```php
// Good: the value is sent separately from the SQL
$stmt = $pdo->prepare('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ?');
$stmt->execute([$email]);
```
- Set `PDO::ATTR_EMULATE_PREPARES => false` so MySQL does real server-side prepares.
- Table/column names CAN'T be bound. For dynamic `ORDER BY`, use an allowlist:
```php
$allowed = ['title', 'created_at'];
$sort = in_array($_GET['sort'] ?? '', $allowed, true) ? $_GET['sort'] : 'created_at';
```

### OTHER INJECTION TYPES
- Shell: avoid `exec()`/`shell_exec()`. If you must, wrap every argument in `escapeshellarg()`.
- Paths: never `include $_GET['page']`. For file downloads, take `basename()`, then check `realpath()` starts with your allowed folder (stops `../../etc/passwd`).
- SSRF (fetching a URL the user gave you): allowlist hosts, block private IP ranges (127.0.0.1, 10.x, 192.168.x, 169.254.169.254 = cloud metadata!).
- XSS is injection into HTML: see the Frontend security section.

### VALIDATION RULES
- Validate on the SERVER. Client-side checks are UX only; anyone can skip them with curl.
- Allowlist over blocklist: "must be 1-255 chars, digits only" beats "must not contain <script>".
- Check type, length, range, format: `filter_var($email, FILTER_VALIDATE_EMAIL)`, `(int)` casts, `ctype_digit()`.
- Validation is not escaping: still use prepared statements and output encoding.

### FILE UPLOADS
Check size, check real type with `finfo`, generate your own filename, store outside the web root (or in a folder where PHP execution is disabled), never trust the client's MIME type.

### SOURCES
- https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/SQL_Injection_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html
- https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Input_Validation_Cheat_Sheet.html
- https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/File_Upload_Cheat_Sheet.html

nodes.title: Passwords & sessions in PHP
nodes.content:
### STORING PASSWORDS
```php
$hash = password_hash($password, PASSWORD_ARGON2ID); // or PASSWORD_DEFAULT (bcrypt)
if (password_verify($input, $hash)) {
    if (password_needs_rehash($hash, PASSWORD_ARGON2ID)) {
        // save a fresh hash: upgrades old hashes over time
    }
}
```
- Never MD5/SHA-256 for passwords: they're fast, which helps attackers.
- OWASP minimums: Argon2id with 19 MiB memory, 2 iterations, parallelism 1. bcrypt: cost 10+ (PHP 8.4 raised the default to 12), and note bcrypt only uses the first 72 bytes.

### PASSWORD RULES (NIST SP 800-63B-4, final 2025)
- Minimum 15 characters when the password is the only factor (8 if MFA is also used).
- Allow at least 64 characters, spaces and Unicode, and pasting from password managers.
- NO composition rules ("1 uppercase + 1 symbol") and NO forced periodic changes.
- DO check new passwords against a breached-password list (e.g. Have I Been Pwned k-anonymity API).

### SESSIONS
```php
session_set_cookie_params([
    'secure' => true,     // HTTPS only
    'httponly' => true,   // JavaScript can't read it
    'samesite' => 'Lax',  // not sent on most cross-site requests
]);
ini_set('session.use_strict_mode', '1'); // reject made-up session IDs
session_start();

// After a successful login (and on any privilege change):
session_regenerate_id(true); // stops session fixation
```
- Idle timeout (e.g. 30 min) AND absolute timeout (e.g. 12 h), enforced server-side with timestamps in `$_SESSION`.
- Logout: `$_SESSION = []`, `session_destroy()`, expire the cookie.

### LOGIN FLOW HYGIENE
- Same error for "no such user" and "wrong password" (no account enumeration).
- Throttle by account AND by IP; add increasing delays instead of permanent lockouts (lockouts let attackers lock out real users).
- Password reset tokens: random (`bin2hex(random_bytes(32))`), stored hashed, single-use, expire in ~30 minutes.

### SOURCES
- https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Password_Storage_Cheat_Sheet.html
- https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html
- https://www.php.net/manual/en/features.session.security.management.php
- https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Session_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html

nodes.title: Access control: stop IDOR
nodes.content:
### THE #1 RISK
Broken Access Control is A01 in the OWASP Top 10:2025, and its API cousin "Broken Object Level Authorization" (BOLA) is API1 in the OWASP API Top 10. Logging in proves WHO you are; access control decides WHAT you may touch.

### IDOR IN ONE EXAMPLE
`GET /api/get-invoice.php?id=1043` returns invoice 1043. The attacker tries 1044, 1045... and reads everyone's invoices. The fix is a check on EVERY request:
```php
$stmt = $pdo->prepare('SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE id = ? AND user_id = ?');
$stmt->execute([$id, $_SESSION['user_id']]);
$invoice = $stmt->fetch();
if (!$invoice) {
    http_response_code(404); // don't reveal that it exists
    exit;
}
```
Random IDs (UUIDs) make guessing harder, but they are NOT access control.

### RULES
- Deny by default. Every endpoint starts locked; you open it deliberately.
- Enforce on the server, in one place (a `require_owner()` / `require_role()` helper), not scattered ifs.
- Never trust role, user_id or price fields sent by the client. Take user_id from the session.
- Check the function too: is a normal user calling `delete-user.php`? (Function-level authorization.)
- Mass assignment: don't blindly copy `$_POST` into an UPDATE. Allowlist the fields a user may change, or someone sends `is_admin=1`.
- Hiding a button in the UI is not security; the endpoint must refuse.

### RBAC VS ABAC
- RBAC (roles): admin, editor, viewer. Simple, fits most apps.
- ABAC (attributes): "owner of the record, or member of the same team, during office hours". More flexible, more complex.

### TEST IT
Write tests where user A tries to read/update/delete user B's records and expect 403/404. These are the most valuable security tests you can have.

### SOURCES
- https://owasp.org/Top10/2025/
- https://owasp.org/API-Security/editions/2023/en/0xa1-broken-object-level-authorization/
- https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Authorization_Cheat_Sheet.html

nodes.title: Secrets, config & dependencies (supply chain)
nodes.content:
### MISCONFIGURATION (A02, now #2)
- Production PHP: `display_errors=Off`, `log_errors=On`, `expose_php=Off`.
- Apache: `Options -Indexes` (no directory listings), deny access to `.env`, `.git`, backups (`*.sql`, `*.bak`).
- No default or shared admin passwords; remove sample/test files from servers.
- Database user for the app gets only the privileges it needs (no DROP, no GRANT).

### SECRETS
- Never commit secrets. Keep them in a config file OUTSIDE the web root, or environment variables, readable only by the app user.
- Use different secrets for dev and prod.
- Turn on secret scanning (GitHub push protection, gitleaks). If a secret leaks, ROTATE it; deleting the commit is not enough.

### SUPPLY CHAIN (A03, new in 2025)
Your app includes code you didn't write. In 2025 the "Shai-Hulud" worm hit npm twice: it stole developer and CI tokens from infected packages, then used them to publish more infected packages. The second wave ran during `preinstall`, so simply installing was enough to get hit.

### DEFENCES
- Commit lock files (`composer.lock`, `package-lock.json`) and install exactly from them (`composer install`, `npm ci`).
- Run `composer audit` / `npm audit` and keep dependencies updated, but don't auto-merge brand-new releases blindly; a short delay lets the community catch malware.
- Disable install scripts where you can (`npm ci --ignore-scripts`; pnpm 10 blocks dependency scripts by default).
- Fewer dependencies = smaller attack surface. Vendoring a static file (like a `lib/` folder of downloaded library files) is fine: record its version and source.
- Loading from a CDN? Add Subresource Integrity: `<script src="..." integrity="sha384-..." crossorigin="anonymous">`.
- Protect CI: least-privilege tokens, phishing-resistant MFA on npm/GitHub accounts, pin third-party GitHub Actions to a commit SHA.

### SOURCES
- https://owasp.org/Top10/2025/
- https://www.infoworld.com/article/4095604/new-shai-hulud-worm-spreading-through-npm-github-2.html
- https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Subresource_Integrity
- https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Secrets_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html

nodes.title: Rate limiting, logging & safe errors
nodes.content:
### RATE LIMITING
Protects logins, password resets, 2FA checks, signups and expensive endpoints from brute force and abuse.
- Key the limit by account AND IP (attackers rotate IPs; shared offices share IPs).
- Respond `429 Too Many Requests` with a `Retry-After` header.
- Simple PHP approach: a table `(key, window_start, count)` or Redis `INCR` + `EXPIRE`. The API section covers the algorithms.

### LOGGING THAT HELPS (A09)
The 2025 rename to "Security Logging & ALERTING Failures" makes a point: logs nobody watches don't catch attacks.
Log:
- Logins (success and failure), logouts, password/2FA changes
- Access-control denials (403s), validation failures at unusual rates
- Admin actions (who changed what, when)
Never log: passwords, session IDs, tokens, OTP codes, full card numbers.
Alert on: spikes of failed logins, many 403s from one user, admin logins from new places.

### FAIL CLOSED (A10, new in 2025)
"Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions": when something unexpected happens, the safe answer is NO.
```php
try {
    $allowed = user_can_edit($userId, $noteId);
} catch (Throwable $e) {
    error_log($e->getMessage());
    $allowed = false; // an error in the permission check must not grant access
}
```
- Show users a generic message ("Something went wrong"); keep the stack trace in the server log.
- Don't leave half-finished work: use transactions so an error rolls everything back.
- Handle timeouts, empty results and null values explicitly instead of assuming the happy path.

### SOURCES
- https://owasp.org/Top10/2025/
- https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Logging_Cheat_Sheet.html
- https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Error_Handling_Cheat_Sheet.html

nodes.title: XSS & Content Security Policy
nodes.content:
### WHAT XSS IS
An attacker gets THEIR JavaScript running on YOUR page, as your user: it can read the page, call your API with the user's cookies, and phish them.
- Stored: saved in the DB (a comment), shown to others
- Reflected: bounced back from the URL (`?q=<script>...`)
- DOM-based: your own JS puts untrusted data into the page

### RULE 1: ENCODE OUTPUT FOR ITS CONTEXT
- PHP into HTML: `htmlspecialchars($value)` (PHP 8.1+ defaults to ENT_QUOTES | ENT_SUBSTITUTE, so quotes are covered).
- JS: use `textContent`, not `innerHTML`.
- Vue: `{{ value }}` escapes automatically; `v-html` does NOT.
- URLs: only allow `http:`/`https:` in user-supplied links (block `javascript:`).

### RULE 2: SANITIZE WHEN YOU MUST RENDER HTML
User Markdown or rich text: render it, then sanitize with DOMPurify before inserting. (Evolve does exactly this in `src/markdown.js`.)

### RULE 3: A STRICT CSP AS A SAFETY NET
A Content Security Policy tells the browser which scripts may run. Google's recommended "strict CSP" uses a random nonce per response:
```
Content-Security-Policy:
  script-src 'nonce-R4nd0m' 'strict-dynamic';
  object-src 'none';
  base-uri 'none';
```
```php
$nonce = base64_encode(random_bytes(16)); // new for EVERY response
header("Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'nonce-$nonce' 'strict-dynamic'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'none'");
echo "<script nonce=\"$nonce\" src=\"app.js\"></script>";
```
- `strict-dynamic` lets your trusted scripts load further scripts, so libraries keep working.
- Avoid URL allowlists (`script-src cdn.example.com`): they are easy to bypass.
- Roll out with `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only` first and watch the reports.

### TRUSTED TYPES (Baseline 2026)
Now supported in all major browsers: `require-trusted-types-for 'script'` makes the browser reject raw strings passed to `innerHTML` and similar sinks unless they went through a policy (e.g. DOMPurify). It removes DOM XSS at the source.

### SOURCES
- https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cross_Site_Scripting_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html
- https://web.dev/articles/strict-csp
- https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Trusted_Types_API
- https://web.dev/baseline/2026

nodes.title: CSRF, CORS & SameSite cookies
nodes.content:
### CSRF IN ONE SENTENCE
Another site makes the user's browser send a request to YOUR site, and the browser attaches your cookies, so the request looks legitimate ("transfer money", "change email").

### THE DEFENCES (OWASP cheat sheet, current)
1. CSRF tokens: a random token in the session, echoed in every form/AJAX request, compared with `hash_equals()`. Still the classic answer.
2. Fetch Metadata: browsers send `Sec-Fetch-Site` (`same-origin`, `same-site`, `cross-site`, `none`). JavaScript can't fake it. OWASP now lists it as a primary defence for modern browsers, with an Origin/Referer check as the fallback when the header is missing.
3. SameSite cookies: defence in depth, not a full fix on their own.
4. Custom request header for AJAX (e.g. `X-Requested-With`): cross-site requests with custom headers trigger a CORS preflight, which you won't allow.

```php
// Reject cross-site state-changing requests
$site = $_SERVER['HTTP_SEC_FETCH_SITE'] ?? null;
if ($_SERVER['REQUEST_METHOD'] !== 'GET') {
    if ($site !== null && $site !== 'same-origin') {
        http_response_code(403);
        exit;
    }
    // Header missing (old browser): fall back to checking the Origin header
}
```

### SAMESITE
- `Lax` (the browser default for cookies without the attribute): sent on top-level navigations, not on cross-site POSTs or fetches. GET must therefore NEVER change data.
- `Strict`: never sent cross-site. Safest, but users arriving from an external link look logged out on that first page.
- `None; Secure`: needed only for genuine cross-site use (embedded widgets).
- "Same site" means same registrable domain, so `evil.example.com` counts as same-site with `app.example.com`.

### CORS IS NOT A SECURITY FEATURE
CORS relaxes the browser's same-origin policy; it doesn't protect your API (curl ignores it).
- Don't reflect any `Origin` back with `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`.
- Allowlist exact origins; avoid `*.example.com` patterns.

### SOURCES
- https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cross-Site_Request_Forgery_Prevention_Cheat_Sheet.html
- https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/Security/Attacks/CSRF
- https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/CORS

nodes.title: Tokens in the browser: where to keep them
nodes.content:
### THE QUESTION
Your frontend needs to prove who the user is on every API call. Where does that proof live?

### OPTION 1 (BEST FOR MOST APPS): A SESSION COOKIE
Same-site PHP app or Vue SPA served from the same domain as its API? Use a plain server session:
- Cookie: `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax`
- JavaScript never sees it, so XSS can't steal it (XSS can still USE it while the page is open, which is why XSS prevention still matters).
- Add CSRF protection (previous leaf).

### OPTION 2: BACKEND-FOR-FRONTEND (BFF)
Your SPA uses OAuth/OIDC (e.g. "Sign in with Google") or a third-party API. A small server-side component does the OAuth dance, keeps the access/refresh tokens on the server, and gives the browser only a session cookie. The IETF's "OAuth 2.0 for Browser-Based Applications" guidance recommends this as the most secure pattern.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    SPA["Vue SPA"] -->|"session cookie (HttpOnly)"| BFF["BFF (PHP)"]
    BFF -->|"access token (never in browser)"| API["Third-party API"]
    BFF <-->|"OAuth / OIDC"| IDP["Identity provider"]
```

### OPTION 3 (WHEN YOU MUST): TOKENS IN JAVASCRIPT
- Access token in memory only (a JS variable), short-lived (5-15 min).
- Refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie, rotated on every use.
- Avoid `localStorage` for tokens: any XSS anywhere on the origin can read it and send it to the attacker, who can then use it from their own machine for as long as it's valid.

### JWT GOTCHAS
- A JWT is signed, not encrypted: anyone can read its contents (base64). Don't put secrets in it.
- Verify the signature and pin the algorithm (reject `alg: none`).
- You can't easily revoke a JWT before it expires; keep them short-lived, or use plain sessions.

### SOURCES
- https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-oauth-browser-based-apps/
- https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/HTML5_Security_Cheat_Sheet.html
- https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/JSON_Web_Token_for_Java_Cheat_Sheet.html

nodes.title: Security headers checklist
nodes.content:
### WHY
A few response headers switch on browser protections for free. Set them once in Apache and every page benefits.

### OWASP'S RECOMMENDED VALUES
| Header | Value | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Strict-Transport-Security | `max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload` | Browser only ever uses HTTPS for your site |
| Content-Security-Policy | see the XSS leaf | Limits which scripts run |
| X-Content-Type-Options | `nosniff` | Stops the browser guessing file types |
| Referrer-Policy | `strict-origin-when-cross-origin` | Doesn't leak full URLs to other sites |
| Permissions-Policy | `geolocation=(), camera=(), microphone=()` | Disables features you don't use |
| CSP frame-ancestors / X-Frame-Options | `frame-ancestors 'none'` / `DENY` | Stops clickjacking via iframes |
| Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy | `same-origin` | Isolates your window from popups |
| X-XSS-Protection | don't set (or `0`) | Old filter, now harmful |
| Server / X-Powered-By | remove | Don't advertise versions |

### APACHE EXAMPLE
```apache
Header always set Strict-Transport-Security "max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains"
Header always set X-Content-Type-Options "nosniff"
Header always set Referrer-Policy "strict-origin-when-cross-origin"
Header always set Permissions-Policy "geolocation=(), camera=(), microphone=()"
Header always set Content-Security-Policy "frame-ancestors 'none'"
Header always unset X-Powered-By
ServerTokens Prod
ServerSignature Off
```
(Needs `a2enmod headers`. In PHP, also set `expose_php = Off`.)

### CAREFUL WITH
- HSTS `preload`: once you're on the browser preload list, every subdomain must have HTTPS. Hard to undo.
- `Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp`: only if you need cross-origin isolation (SharedArrayBuffer); it can break third-party images and embeds.
- LAN-only HTTP apps: HSTS only works over HTTPS, so it does nothing there.

### CHECK YOUR SITE
Mozilla HTTP Observatory (now on MDN) and securityheaders.com grade your headers.

### SOURCES
- https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/HTTP_Headers_Cheat_Sheet.html
- https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/observatory
- https://hstspreload.org/

nodes.title: Crypto basics: hashing, symmetric, asymmetric
nodes.content:
### FIVE TOOLS, FIVE JOBS
| Tool | Job | Reversible? | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hash | Fingerprint / integrity check | No | SHA-256, BLAKE2 |
| Password hash | Store passwords | No (deliberately slow) | Argon2id, bcrypt |
| HMAC | Prove data wasn't changed + came from a key holder | No | HMAC-SHA256 |
| Symmetric encryption | Hide data; same key locks and unlocks | Yes | AES-256-GCM, XChaCha20-Poly1305 |
| Asymmetric | Key exchange & signatures with a public/private key pair | Yes / verify | X25519, Ed25519, RSA |

Encoding (base64, hex) is NOT encryption: anyone can decode it.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Q{"What do you need?"} -->|"Store a password"| P["Argon2id / bcrypt"]
    Q -->|"Detect tampering"| H["HMAC-SHA256"]
    Q -->|"Hide data you'll read later"| S["AEAD: XChaCha20-Poly1305 or AES-GCM"]
    Q -->|"Others must verify it's from you"| G["Signature: Ed25519"]
    Q -->|"Agree a key over the internet"| K["Key exchange: X25519 (inside TLS)"]
```

### AUTHENTICATED ENCRYPTION (AEAD)
Modern symmetric encryption both hides the data AND detects tampering. Decryption fails if one byte was changed. Use AEAD modes only: AES-GCM or (X)ChaCha20-Poly1305. Never ECB, and never CBC without a MAC.

### NONCES & IVs
Most ciphers need a unique random "number used once" per message. It doesn't need to be secret (store it next to the ciphertext) but it must NEVER repeat with the same key. With AES-GCM a repeat is catastrophic; XChaCha20's 24-byte nonce makes random nonces safe.

### RANDOMNESS
Use a cryptographically secure generator only: PHP `random_bytes()` / `random_int()`, JS `crypto.getRandomValues()` / `crypto.randomUUID()`. Never `rand()`, `mt_rand()` or `Math.random()` for anything security-related.

### THE GOLDEN RULE
Don't invent your own crypto. Use a high-level, hard-to-misuse library: libsodium (`sodium_*` functions, built into PHP since 7.2) on the server, the Web Crypto API in the browser.

### SOURCES
- https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Cryptographic_Storage_Cheat_Sheet.html
- https://paragonie.com/book/pecl-libsodium
- https://www.php.net/manual/en/book.sodium.php

nodes.title: HTTPS & TLS (including post-quantum)
nodes.content:
### WHAT TLS GIVES YOU
- Confidentiality: nobody on the network can read the traffic
- Integrity: nobody can change it in transit
- Authentication: the certificate proves you're talking to the real server

### HOW A TLS 1.3 CONNECTION STARTS
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser
    participant S as Server
    B->>S: ClientHello (supported ciphers + key share)
    S->>B: ServerHello (its key share) + certificate + signature
    Note over B,S: Both sides derive the same session keys (key exchange)
    B->>S: Encrypted HTTP request
    S->>B: Encrypted HTTP response
```
TLS 1.3 needs just one round trip, removed old weak ciphers, and should be your minimum together with TLS 1.2. Turn off TLS 1.0/1.1.

### CERTIFICATES IN PRACTICE
- Let's Encrypt + certbot (`certbot --apache`) gives free certificates and renews them automatically.
- Certificate lifetimes are shrinking (CA/Browser Forum, 2025 vote): max 200 days from March 2026, 100 days from 2027, 47 days by 2029. Manual renewal is no longer realistic: automate it.
- Redirect all HTTP to HTTPS, then add HSTS.
- Avoid "mixed content" (HTTP images/scripts on HTTPS pages).

### POST-QUANTUM TLS (ALREADY HAPPENING)
Large quantum computers could one day break today's key exchange. Attackers can record encrypted traffic now and decrypt it later ("harvest now, decrypt later").
- The hybrid key exchange X25519MLKEM768 (classic X25519 + the new NIST standard ML-KEM) is on by default in Chrome and Firefox.
- OpenSSL 3.5+ supports it, so updated servers negotiate it automatically.
- Certificates and signatures are still classical for now; that migration comes later.
What you do: keep your OS, OpenSSL and Apache updated. That's it for most apps.

### INSIDE YOUR NETWORK
"It's internal" isn't a reason to skip TLS once data crosses machines you don't fully control (cloud networks, database connections between hosts).

### SOURCES
- https://letsencrypt.org/docs/
- https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Transport_Layer_Security_Cheat_Sheet.html
- https://ssl-config.mozilla.org/
- https://blog.cloudflare.com/pq-2025/

nodes.title: Encrypting data at rest in PHP (sodium)
Encryption in the browser (Web Crypto API)
Key management & rotation
nodes.content:
### ENCRYPTION IS ONLY AS GOOD AS ITS KEYS
A key stored next to the data it protects (same DB, same backup, same git repo) protects nothing.

### WHERE KEYS LIVE (from simple to strong)
1. A config file outside the web root, permissions `600`, owned by the app user. Fine for a single small server.
2. Environment variables injected at deploy time.
3. A secrets manager: AWS Secrets Manager, HashiCorp Vault, Doppler.
4. A KMS / HSM (AWS KMS, Google Cloud KMS): the master key never leaves special hardware; you ask it to encrypt/decrypt.

### ENVELOPE ENCRYPTION (how KMS-based systems work)
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    KMS["KMS master key (KEK) - never leaves KMS"] -->|"encrypts"| DEK["Data key (DEK)"]
    DEK -->|"encrypts"| DATA[("Your data")]
    DEKE["Encrypted DEK stored next to data"] -.->|"ask KMS to decrypt"| KMS
```
- Each file or record gets a data key; the data key is stored encrypted by the master key.
- Rotating the master key only means re-encrypting the small data keys, not all the data.

### ROTATION
- Tag every ciphertext with a key ID (`v1:`, `v2:`).
- New writes use the newest key; reads pick the key by its ID.
- Re-encrypt old records in a background job, then retire the old key.
- Rotate immediately if a key may have leaked.

### OTHER RULES
- One key per purpose (encryption key ≠ blind-index key ≠ session-signing key). Derive sub-keys with `sodium_crypto_kdf_derive_from_key()` if you only want to manage one master secret.
- Back up keys separately from data backups, and test restoring both.
- Log who/what accessed keys (KMS does this for you via CloudTrail).

### SOURCES
- https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Key_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html
- https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/kms-cryptography.html#enveloping
- https://www.php.net/manual/en/function.sodium-crypto-kdf-derive-from-key.php

nodes.title: How TOTP works (RFC 6238)
nodes.content:
### THE IDEA
The server and the user's authenticator app share a secret. Both compute a 6-digit code from that secret plus the current time. If the codes match, the user has the device.

### THE ALGORITHM
1. Secret: random bytes (RFC recommends 160 bits = 20 bytes), shown to the user as base32 inside a QR code.
2. Time step: `counter = floor(unix_time / 30)`.
3. `HMAC-SHA1(secret, counter)` gives 20 bytes.
4. "Dynamic truncation": pick 4 bytes based on the last nibble, turn them into a number.
5. `number % 1,000,000`, padded to 6 digits.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant A as Authenticator app
    participant S as Server
    S->>U: QR code (otpauth://totp/... with secret)
    U->>A: Scan once, the app stores the secret
    Note over A,S: Later, at login...
    A->>U: Code from HMAC(secret, time/30)
    U->>S: Password + 6-digit code
    S->>S: Compute codes for steps now-1, now, now+1 and compare
```

### THE QR CODE CONTENT
```
otpauth://totp/MyApp:alice@example.com?secret=JBSWY3DPEHPK3PXP&issuer=MyApp
```
Stick to the defaults (SHA1, 6 digits, 30 s): some apps ignore other settings. SHA1 is still fine here because HMAC-SHA1 isn't affected by SHA1's collision weakness.

### VERIFICATION RULES
- Accept at most one step either side of "now" (±30 s) for clock drift. Wider windows help brute-force attackers.
- Keep the server clock synced (NTP).
- Each code works ONCE: remember the last accepted time step per user and reject anything at or below it.
- Rate-limit attempts: 6 digits = 1 million options; unlimited guessing breaks it.

### LIMITS
TOTP stops password-only attacks (leaked or reused passwords). It is NOT phishing-resistant: a fake login page can ask for the code and use it within 30 seconds. Passkeys fix that.

### SOURCES
- https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc6238
- https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc4226
- https://github.com/google/google-authenticator/wiki/Key-Uri-Format
- https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Multifactor_Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.html

nodes.title: Implementing TOTP in PHP
Recovery codes, resets & 2FA UX
nodes.content:
### RECOVERY CODES
People lose phones. Without a recovery path, 2FA becomes a support nightmare, or a weak "reset" that bypasses 2FA entirely.
- Generate 8-10 codes at enrolment, e.g. `bin2hex(random_bytes(5))` formatted as `a3f9-c21e04`.
- Show them ONCE; offer download/print; suggest storing them in a password manager.
- Store them HASHED (`password_hash`), like passwords. Mark each as used after one use.
- "Regenerate codes" invalidates all old ones.
- Warn the user when they're running low.

### RULES FROM THE OWASP MFA CHEAT SHEET
- Changing or removing a factor requires re-authentication with an existing factor, not just an active session.
- Notify the user by email whenever 2FA is enabled, disabled or changed, and on failed 2FA attempts after a correct password (a sign their password is known).
- Ask for 2FA on sensitive actions too (step-up): changing email or password, disabling 2FA, admin areas.
- Enforce 2FA for admins and privileged users; cover EVERY login path (API, mobile app), not just the web form.
- SMS is a "restricted" authenticator (SIM swapping, interception). Offer TOTP or passkeys instead; never SMS-only for sensitive data.
- Security questions don't count as a factor.

### UX THAT PEOPLE ACCEPT
- `<input inputmode="numeric" autocomplete="one-time-code" maxlength="6">` gives a number pad and lets phones autofill.
- Accept codes typed with spaces ("123 456"); strip them first.
- "Remember this device for 30 days": a signed, HttpOnly cookie tied to the user; list and revoke remembered devices in settings.
- Clear messages: "That code didn't work. Codes change every 30 seconds; check your phone's time is automatic."

### ACCOUNT RECOVERY WITHOUT CODES
Have a deliberate, slower process (identity checks, a waiting period with email notifications) so it can't be used as a 2FA bypass.

### SOURCES
- https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Multifactor_Authentication_Cheat_Sheet.html
- https://docs.github.com/en/authentication/securing-your-account-with-two-factor-authentication-2fa/configuring-two-factor-authentication-recovery-methods
- https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Attributes/autocomplete

nodes.title: Passkeys (WebAuthn): the 2026 default
nodes.content:
### WHAT A PASSKEY IS
A key pair created by the user's device for YOUR site. The private key stays in the phone, laptop or password manager (synced via iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager, 1Password...). Your server stores only the public key. Login = the device signs a random challenge after a fingerprint, face or PIN check.

### WHY EVERYONE IS MOVING
- Phishing-resistant: the browser only uses the passkey on the real domain, so a fake site gets nothing.
- Nothing to leak: a database breach exposes only public keys.
- Faster for users: FIDO reports ~93% login success vs ~63% for traditional MFA.
- Mainstream: ~5 billion passkeys in use (FIDO Alliance, World Passkey Day 2026). NIST SP 800-63B-4 accepts synced passkeys at AAL2.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant B as Browser + device
    participant S as Your server
    B->>S: I want to log in
    S->>B: Random challenge
    B->>B: User unlocks with fingerprint / face / PIN
    B->>S: Challenge signed with the private key
    S->>S: Verify with stored public key -> logged in
```

### THE TWO CEREMONIES
- Registration: `navigator.credentials.create({ publicKey: options })`. The server sends a challenge, its RP ID (your domain) and user info; it stores the returned credential ID and public key.
- Login: `navigator.credentials.get({ publicKey: options })`. The server verifies the signature against the stored public key and checks the challenge.
Use a library for the server-side verification (CBOR parsing, signature checks): `web-auth/webauthn-lib` or the lightweight `lbuchs/WebAuthn` for PHP; SimpleWebAuthn for Node.

### PASSKEY AUTOFILL (conditional UI)
```html
<input name="username" autocomplete="username webauthn">
```
```js
if (await PublicKeyCredential.isConditionalMediationAvailable?.()) {
  const cred = await navigator.credentials.get({ publicKey: options, mediation: 'conditional' });
}
```
The browser offers saved passkeys right in the username field's autofill.

### ROLLOUT STRATEGY
1. Add "Create a passkey" in account settings (and offer it after a successful password login).
2. Keep password + TOTP as a fallback; let users register several passkeys.
3. Later, let users go passwordless.
Passkeys need HTTPS and a real domain (localhost works for development).

### SOURCES
- https://fidoalliance.org/fido-alliance-reports-accelerating-global-passkey-adoption-on-world-passkey-day-2026/
- https://web.dev/articles/passkey-form-autofill
- https://passkeys.dev/
- https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Web_Authentication_API

### THE GOLDEN RULE OF SCALING

nodes.title: Relational modelling & normalisation
nodes.content:
### THE BUILDING BLOCKS
- Table = one kind of thing (users, notes). Row = one instance. Column = one fact about it.
- Primary key (PK): uniquely identifies a row (`id INT UNSIGNED AUTO_INCREMENT`).
- Foreign key (FK): points at another table's PK and keeps references valid.

```mermaid
erDiagram
    USERS ||--o{ NOTES : writes
    NOTES ||--o{ NOTE_TAGS : has
    TAGS ||--o{ NOTE_TAGS : labels
    USERS {
        int id PK
        string email
    }
    NOTES {
        int id PK
        int user_id FK
        string title
    }
    TAGS {
        int id PK
        string name
    }
    NOTE_TAGS {
        int note_id FK
        int tag_id FK
    }
```

### RELATIONSHIPS
- One-to-many: a FK on the "many" side (`notes.user_id`).
- Many-to-many: a join table (`note_tags`) with a composite PK `(note_id, tag_id)`.
- One-to-one: rare; usually just more columns, or a FK with UNIQUE.

### NORMALISATION IN PLAIN WORDS
- 1NF: one value per cell; no `tags = "php,sql,vue"` strings.
- 2NF/3NF: every column depends on the key, the whole key and nothing but the key. Don't store the user's email on every note; store `user_id` and join.
Why: each fact lives in ONE place, so updates can't create contradictions.
When to denormalise: measured read performance problems, reporting tables, caching a count. Do it deliberately and keep it in sync.

### CONSTRAINTS ARE FREE BUG CATCHERS
`NOT NULL`, `UNIQUE (email)`, `CHECK (amount >= 0)`, FKs with `ON DELETE CASCADE` or `RESTRICT`. The database enforces them even if your PHP has a bug. (A `notes.folder_id` FK with CASCADE, for example, means deleting a folder deletes its notes.)

### DATA TYPE CHOICES
- Money: `DECIMAL(12,2)`, never FLOAT.
- Text: `utf8mb4` (real UTF-8 incl. emoji; the default in MariaDB 11.8).
- Dates: `DATETIME` for "wall clock" values; `TIMESTAMP` converts to UTC (MariaDB 11.8 extended its range to 2106).
- Booleans: `TINYINT(1)`.
- IDs: auto-increment ints, or UUIDv7 (time-ordered, so index-friendly) if IDs are created outside the DB.

### SOURCES
- https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/ddl-constraints.html
- https://mariadb.com/kb/en/database-normalization/
- https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9562 (UUIDv7)

nodes.title: Indexes: how they work
nodes.content:
### THE PHONE BOOK ANALOGY
Without an index, `WHERE email = ?` reads every row (a "full table scan"). An index is a sorted copy of some columns (a B-tree) with pointers back to the rows: the database jumps straight to the match. Millions of rows: milliseconds instead of seconds.

### WHAT TO INDEX
- Columns in `WHERE`, `JOIN ... ON`, and `ORDER BY` of frequent queries
- Foreign keys (InnoDB adds these automatically)
- `UNIQUE` columns (the constraint creates an index)

### COMPOSITE INDEXES: THE LEFTMOST RULE
An index on `(user_id, created_at)` helps:
- `WHERE user_id = 5`
- `WHERE user_id = 5 AND created_at > '2026-01-01'`
- `WHERE user_id = 5 ORDER BY created_at DESC`
It does NOT help `WHERE created_at > ...` alone (it skips the first column).
Order columns: equality filters first, range/sort columns last.

### COVERING INDEXES
If the index contains every column the query needs, the table isn't read at all (`EXPLAIN` shows "Using index"). Great for hot read queries; costs disk and write speed.

### THINGS THAT SILENTLY DISABLE AN INDEX
- Functions on the column: `WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2026` -> write `created_at >= '2026-01-01' AND created_at < '2027-01-01'`
- Leading wildcards: `LIKE '%term'` (use FULLTEXT search instead)
- Type mismatches: comparing a VARCHAR column to a number
- `OR` across different columns (sometimes)

### THE COST
Every index slows INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE and uses space. Don't index everything; drop indexes no query uses. An index on `(a, b)` already covers queries on `a` alone, so a separate index on `a` is redundant.

### LOW-CARDINALITY COLUMNS
An index on a boolean `completed` column rarely helps on its own (half the rows match), but it can be useful as the SECOND column of a composite index.

### SOURCES
- https://use-the-index-luke.com/
- https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/optimization-indexes.html
- https://mariadb.com/kb/en/optimization-and-indexes/

nodes.title: Reading EXPLAIN & fixing slow queries
nodes.content:
### STEP 1: FIND THE SLOW QUERIES
Turn on the slow query log (`slow_query_log=1`, `long_query_time=0.5`) and look at the worst offenders by total time, not just single slow runs.

### STEP 2: EXPLAIN
```sql
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM notes WHERE user_id = 5 ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 20;
```
| Column | Look for |
|---|---|
| type | `ALL` = full scan (bad on big tables); `ref`/`range`/`eq_ref`/`const` = using an index |
| key | which index was chosen (NULL = none) |
| rows | estimated rows examined; compare with rows returned |
| Extra | `Using filesort` / `Using temporary` = extra sorting work; `Using index` = covering index |

`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` (MySQL 8) or `ANALYZE SELECT ...` (MariaDB) actually runs the query and shows real timings. PostgreSQL: `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)`.

### THE USUAL FIXES
1. Add or adjust an index (often a composite one matching WHERE + ORDER BY).
2. Select only needed columns instead of `SELECT *`.
3. Rewrite the condition so it can use the index (no functions on columns).
4. Paginate with a "keyset" instead of big OFFSETs:
```sql
-- OFFSET 100000 reads and throws away 100k rows:
SELECT * FROM notes ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000;
-- Keyset: remember the last id you showed
SELECT * FROM notes WHERE id < 48213 ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20;
```

### THE N+1 PROBLEM (the most common app-side cause)
```php
$notes = $pdo->query('SELECT * FROM notes')->fetchAll();
foreach ($notes as $note) {
    // one extra query PER note: 1 + N queries
    $tags = get_tags_for_note($note['id']);
}
```
Fix: one query with a JOIN, or `WHERE note_id IN (...)` for all notes at once.

### MEASURE AGAIN
Check the fix with EXPLAIN and real timings. Sometimes the optimizer ignores your index because it estimates a scan is cheaper; run `ANALYZE TABLE` to refresh statistics.

### SOURCES
- https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/using-explain.html
- https://mariadb.com/kb/en/explain/
- https://use-the-index-luke.com/no-offset

nodes.title: Transactions, ACID & isolation levels
nodes.content:
### ACID
- Atomic: all statements succeed or none do
- Consistent: constraints hold before and after
- Isolated: concurrent transactions don't see each other's half-done work (to a degree: see levels)
- Durable: once committed, it survives a crash

### IN PHP
```php
$pdo->beginTransaction();
try {
    $pdo->prepare('UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - ? WHERE id = ?')->execute([$amount, $from]);
    $pdo->prepare('UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + ? WHERE id = ?')->execute([$amount, $to]);
    $pdo->commit();
} catch (Throwable $e) {
    $pdo->rollBack();
    throw $e;
}
```

### ISOLATION LEVELS
| Level | Dirty read | Non-repeatable read | Phantom rows |
|---|---|---|---|
| READ UNCOMMITTED | possible | possible | possible |
| READ COMMITTED (PostgreSQL default) | no | possible | possible |
| REPEATABLE READ (MySQL/MariaDB InnoDB default) | no | no | mostly no* |
| SERIALIZABLE | no | no | no |
- Dirty read: seeing uncommitted data. Non-repeatable: same row, different value on re-read. Phantom: a re-run query returns new rows.
- *InnoDB plain SELECTs read a consistent snapshot; locking reads use gap locks to block phantoms.

### THE LOST UPDATE (classic bug)
Two requests read stock = 5, both subtract 1, both write 4. One sale vanished. Fixes:
1. Atomic SQL: `UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id = ? AND stock > 0` (check affected rows).
2. Pessimistic lock: `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` inside a transaction.
3. Optimistic lock: a `version` column; `UPDATE ... SET version = version + 1 WHERE id = ? AND version = ?`; if 0 rows changed, someone else won: reload and retry.

### DEADLOCKS
Two transactions each wait for a lock the other holds; the DB kills one (MySQL error 1213). Normal under load: keep transactions short, touch rows in a consistent order, and retry the failed transaction.

### SOURCES
- https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/innodb-transaction-isolation-levels.html
- https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html
- https://www.percona.com/blog/various-types-of-innodb-transaction-isolation-levels-explained-using-terminal/

nodes.title: SQL vs NoSQL (and vectors in SQL)
nodes.content:
### THE FAMILIES
| Type | Model | Good at | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| Relational | Tables + SQL + joins | Most business apps, consistency | MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, SQLite |
| Document | JSON documents | Flexible, nested records | MongoDB, Firestore |
| Key-value | key -> value | Caches, sessions, counters | Redis/Valkey, DynamoDB |
| Wide-column | Huge distributed tables | Massive write volume | Cassandra, ScyllaDB |
| Graph | Nodes + edges | Relationship-heavy queries | Neo4j |
| Search | Inverted index | Full-text search, facets | Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Meilisearch |
| Vector | Embeddings | AI similarity search | pgvector, MariaDB Vector, Qdrant |

### THE PRAGMATIC 2026 ANSWER
Start relational. Modern SQL databases cover most "NoSQL" needs:
- JSON columns with functions/indexes (MySQL/MariaDB `JSON`, PostgreSQL `JSONB`)
- Full-text search (`FULLTEXT` indexes, PostgreSQL `tsvector`)
- Vector search: MariaDB 11.8 LTS has a native `VECTOR` type and index; PostgreSQL has pgvector; MySQL 9 has a VECTOR type but its distance functions are limited to Oracle's HeatWave cloud.
Add a specialised store when you hit a real limit: Redis for caching/queues, a search engine for heavy search.

### CAP IN PRACTICE
In a distributed database, when the network splits you choose: stay Consistent (refuse some requests) or stay Available (serve possibly stale data). Single-server MySQL doesn't face this; it matters with replicas and multi-region setups. Eventual consistency = replicas catch up "soon".

### WHEN NOSQL REALLY WINS
- Simple access patterns at enormous scale (DynamoDB: design tables around your exact queries)
- Data with no fixed shape that you never join
- Caching and ephemeral data (Redis)

### SOURCES
- https://mariadb.org/11-8-lts-released/
- https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector
- https://www.mongodb.com/resources/basics/databases/nosql-explained

nodes.title: Scaling a database: cache, replicas, sharding
nodes.content:
### THE LADDER (climb only as far as you need)
1. Fix queries and indexes (often 10-100x)
2. Bigger server (vertical scaling): more RAM so the working set fits in the buffer pool
3. Cache hot reads (Redis, or plain HTTP caching)
4. Read replicas: copies that serve SELECTs
5. Partitioning: split a huge table by date/range inside one server
6. Sharding: split data across servers by a key (user_id). Last resort: joins and transactions across shards become hard

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    APP["App"] -->|writes| P[("Primary")]
    P -->|replication| R1[("Replica 1")]
    P -->|replication| R2[("Replica 2")]
    APP -->|reads| R1
    APP -->|reads| R2
    APP <-->|"hot data"| C[("Redis cache")]
```

### CACHE-ASIDE PATTERN
```php
$key = "user:$id";
$user = $redis->get($key);
if ($user === false) {
    $user = load_user_from_db($id);
    $redis->setex($key, 300, serialize($user)); // 5-minute TTL
}
```
Invalidate (delete the key) when the user changes. The two hard problems: stale data, and stampedes (many requests rebuilding the same expired key at once; fix with a lock or early refresh).

### REPLICATION GOTCHAS
- Replication lag: a user saves, then reads from a replica that hasn't caught up ("my edit vanished"). Read your own writes from the primary.
- Failover: promoting a replica when the primary dies. Managed services (RDS Multi-AZ) automate it.

### CONNECTIONS
Each PHP request opens a DB connection. At high traffic use connection limits/pooling (ProxySQL, PgBouncer, RDS Proxy).

### SHARDING IN ONE PARAGRAPH
Pick a shard key that spreads load evenly and keeps related data together (user_id: all of a user's notes on one shard). Avoid cross-shard queries. Rebalancing later is painful, which is why "distributed SQL" databases (CockroachDB, TiDB, Aurora DSQL, PlanetScale/Vitess) exist to do it for you.

### SOURCES
- https://github.com/donnemartin/system-design-primer#database
- https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/replication.html
- https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/database-caching-strategies-using-redis/caching-patterns.html

nodes.title: Migrations, backups & recovery
nodes.content:
### SCHEMA MIGRATIONS
Never change production schemas by hand in phpMyAdmin. Keep numbered files in git and apply them in order:
```
migrations/
  001_create_nodes.sql
  002_add_completed_to_nodes.sql
```
A `schema_migrations` table records which have run. Tools: Phinx, Doctrine Migrations, Laravel migrations, Flyway; or a 30-line PHP script.

### ZERO-DOWNTIME CHANGES: EXPAND / CONTRACT
Renaming a column the app uses:
1. Expand: add the new column; write to both
2. Backfill old rows
3. Switch reads to the new column
4. Contract: remove the old column in a later release
Big tables: `ALTER TABLE` can lock for minutes; check if your DB does it "online" (`ALGORITHM=INSTANT/INPLACE`) or use gh-ost / pt-online-schema-change.

### BACKUPS
- Logical: `mariadb-dump --single-transaction --routines dbname | gzip > backup.sql.gz` (consistent for InnoDB without locking).
- Physical: `mariabackup` / Percona XtraBackup for big databases (faster restore).
- Point-in-time recovery: full backup + binary logs lets you restore to "just before the bad DELETE at 14:02".
- 3-2-1 rule: 3 copies, 2 kinds of media, 1 off-site.
- Encrypt backups that leave the machine.

### THE ONLY BACKUP THAT COUNTS IS A TESTED RESTORE
Schedule a restore into a scratch database, check row counts, time it. Know your:
- RPO (recovery point objective): how much data you can afford to lose (1 day? 5 minutes?)
- RTO (recovery time objective): how long you can be down

### SOURCES
- https://mariadb.com/kb/en/mariadb-dump/
- https://mariadb.com/kb/en/mariabackup-overview/
- https://dev.mysql.com/doc/refman/8.4/en/point-in-time-recovery.html

nodes.title: What's new in databases (2025-2026)
nodes.content:
### POSTGRESQL 18 (September 2025)
- New asynchronous I/O system: up to 3x faster reads from storage (io_uring on Linux)
- `uuidv7()` built in: time-ordered UUIDs that index well
- Virtual generated columns (computed at read time) are now the default
- `OLD`/`NEW` values in `RETURNING`, temporal constraints (`WITHOUT OVERLAPS`), OAuth authentication, faster major-version upgrades

### MARIADB 11.8 LTS (June 2025)
- MariaDB Vector: native `VECTOR` type, HNSW-style index, `VEC_DISTANCE_COSINE()`: AI similarity search next to normal tables
- `TIMESTAMP` range extended to 2106 (fixes the year-2038 problem)
- `utf8mb4` is the default character set

### MYSQL
- 8.4 LTS is the conservative choice; the 9.x "Innovation" releases lead to the next LTS line, 9.7 (2026).
- Has a VECTOR type since 9.0, but vector distance functions are only in Oracle's HeatWave cloud.
- Many developers moved to MariaDB or PostgreSQL as Oracle's community investment slowed.

### TRENDS WORTH KNOWING
- PostgreSQL is the default choice for new projects in many teams (extensions: pgvector, PostGIS, TimescaleDB).
- Serverless/branching Postgres: Neon, Supabase, Aurora Serverless; create a DB branch per pull request.
- SQLite in production for small apps (Litestream backups, Turso/libSQL, Cloudflare D1).
- DuckDB: an embedded analytics database that queries CSV/Parquet files with SQL.
- UUIDv7 (RFC 9562, 2024) replacing random UUIDv4 for primary keys.
- AI assistants writing SQL: you still need to read the EXPLAIN plan.

### SOURCES
- https://www.postgresql.org/about/news/postgresql-18-released-3142/
- https://mariadb.org/11-8-lts-released/
- https://www.bytebase.com/blog/what-is-new-in-mysql-9/
- https://duckdb.org/

nodes.title: HTTP essentials for API developers
nodes.content:
### A REQUEST AND A RESPONSE
```
POST /api/notes HTTP/1.1            HTTP/1.1 201 Created
Host: example.com                   Content-Type: application/json
Content-Type: application/json      Location: /api/notes/42
Authorization: Bearer abc123
                                    {"id": 42, "title": "Hi"}
{"title": "Hi"}
```

### METHODS AND THEIR PROMISES
| Method | Use | Safe (no changes) | Idempotent (repeat = same result) |
|---|---|---|---|
| GET | read | yes | yes |
| QUERY | read with a body (complex search) | yes | yes |
| POST | create / run an action | no | no |
| PUT | replace a resource | no | yes |
| PATCH | partial update | no | not necessarily |
| DELETE | remove | no | yes |
QUERY is new: RFC 10008 (June 2026). It's a GET that may carry a request body, for searches too complex for a URL. Support in frameworks and caches is still arriving.
Idempotency matters because networks fail: clients and proxies retry, and a retried PUT/DELETE is harmless while a retried POST may create duplicates.

### STATUS CODES YOU'LL USE DAILY
- 200 OK, 201 Created (+ `Location`), 204 No Content
- 301/308 permanent redirect, 302/307 temporary, 304 Not Modified (cache still valid)
- 400 Bad Request (malformed), 422 Unprocessable Content (valid JSON, failed validation)
- 401 Unauthorized = not logged in; 403 Forbidden = logged in but not allowed
- 404 Not Found, 409 Conflict (version clash, duplicate), 429 Too Many Requests
- 500 bug on your side; 502/503/504 = a proxy or upstream failed / overloaded / timed out

### HEADERS THAT MATTER
`Content-Type`, `Accept`, `Authorization`, `Cache-Control`, `ETag` / `If-None-Match`, `Retry-After`, `Idempotency-Key`.

### HTTP/2 AND HTTP/3
HTTP/2 sends many requests over one connection (no need to bundle everything). HTTP/3 runs over QUIC (UDP): faster connection setup and better on flaky mobile networks. Your PHP code doesn't change; the web server or CDN handles it.

### SOURCES
- https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP
- https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110 (HTTP semantics)
- https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc10008 (QUERY method)

nodes.title: REST API design that ages well
nodes.content:
### RESOURCES, NOT ACTIONS
```
GET    /api/notes            list
POST   /api/notes            create
GET    /api/notes/42         read one
PATCH  /api/notes/42         update
DELETE /api/notes/42         delete
GET    /api/notes/42/tags    sub-resource (keep nesting shallow)
POST   /api/notes/42/archive action that isn't CRUD (acceptable)
```
(An `api/create-note.php` style is RPC-like: also fine for small internal apps. Be consistent either way.)

### LISTS: FILTER, SORT, PAGINATE
- `GET /api/notes?tag=php&sort=-created_at&limit=20`
- Cursor pagination for big or changing lists: return `"next_cursor": "eyJpZCI6NDgyMTN9"`; the client passes it back. Offset pagination (`page=3`) is simpler but slow and skips items when rows are inserted.

### ERRORS: USE RFC 9457 "PROBLEM DETAILS"
The IETF standard error format (replaced RFC 7807 in 2023):
```php
http_response_code(422);
header('Content-Type: application/problem+json');
echo json_encode([
    'type' => 'https://example.com/problems/validation',
    'title' => 'Your request is not valid',
    'status' => 422,
    'detail' => 'Title is required',
    'errors' => [['field' => 'title', 'message' => 'Required']], // extension member
]);
```

### SAFE RETRIES: IDEMPOTENCY KEYS
For POSTs that must not happen twice (payments, orders) the client sends `Idempotency-Key: <uuid>`. The server stores the key with the response; a retry with the same key gets the stored response instead of a second charge. Stripe popularised it; the IETF is standardising the header (draft).

### VERSIONING
Additive changes (new fields) don't need a version. Breaking changes do: `/v2/...` in the URL is the simplest. Never rename or remove a field without one.

### CONSISTENCY CHECKLIST
- One naming style (`snake_case` or `camelCase`), ISO 8601 dates with timezone (`2026-10-14T09:30:00Z`)
- IDs as strings if they might exceed JS's safe integer range
- Return the created/updated object so the client doesn't need another request

### SOURCES
- https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9457
- https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header/
- https://github.com/microsoft/api-guidelines
- https://docs.stripe.com/api/idempotent_requests

nodes.title: API styles: REST, GraphQL, gRPC, WebSockets, SSE
nodes.content:
### THE MENU
| Style | How it works | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| REST / JSON over HTTP | Resources + HTTP verbs | Default for public and web APIs; HTTP caching works |
| GraphQL | One endpoint; client asks for exactly the fields it needs | Many client types with varied data needs (Shopify, GitHub) |
| gRPC | Binary Protocol Buffers over HTTP/2, generated clients | Fast service-to-service calls, streaming |
| tRPC | TypeScript functions called across the network | Full-stack TypeScript monorepos only |
| JSON-RPC | `{"method": "...", "params": ...}` | Simple RPC; MCP (AI tools) uses JSON-RPC 2.0 |
| WebSockets | Persistent two-way connection | Chat, multiplayer, live collaboration |
| Server-Sent Events (SSE) | Server streams events over plain HTTP | Live feeds, notifications, streaming AI responses |
| Webhooks | YOUR server gets an HTTP POST when something happens elsewhere | Payments, GitHub events |

### TRADE-OFFS IN ONE LINE EACH
- GraphQL: no over-fetching, but caching, rate limiting (query cost) and N+1 resolvers get harder.
- gRPC: fast and typed, but browsers need gRPC-Web or a proxy; not human-readable.
- WebSockets: real-time, but stateful connections are harder to load-balance and scale.
- SSE: one-way only, but works through normal HTTP infrastructure and reconnects automatically (`EventSource` in the browser). This is how LLM APIs stream tokens.
- Polling every few seconds is fine for low-traffic dashboards. Don't over-engineer.

### WEBHOOKS DONE RIGHT
- Verify the signature (HMAC of the body with a shared secret) before trusting it.
- Respond 2xx fast, process in the background.
- Expect duplicates and out-of-order delivery: make handlers idempotent (store event IDs).

### SOURCES
- https://graphql.org/learn/
- https://grpc.io/docs/what-is-grpc/introduction/
- https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Server-sent_events
- https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/WebSockets_API

nodes.title: API authentication: keys, JWT, OAuth 2.1
nodes.content:
### WHO IS CALLING?
| Caller | Use |
|---|---|
| Your own web frontend (same site) | Session cookie (see Web Security) |
| Another server / script | API key, or OAuth client credentials |
| A third-party app acting for your user | OAuth 2.x authorization code + PKCE |
| "Log in with Google/GitHub" | OpenID Connect (OIDC) = OAuth + an ID token |
| Internal microservices | mTLS or short-lived signed tokens |

### API KEYS
- Generate with `random_bytes(32)`, show once, store only a HASH (like passwords; SHA-256 is fine for long random keys).
- Add a visible prefix (`mk_live_...`) so leaked keys are easy to spot and secret scanners can detect them.
- Send in a header (`Authorization: Bearer ...`), never in the URL (URLs end up in logs).
- Scopes (read-only vs write), expiry, and a revoke button.

### JWT (JSON WEB TOKENS)
A signed JSON blob: `header.payload.signature`. The server can verify it without a DB lookup.
- Readable by anyone: no secrets inside.
- Keep them short-lived (minutes); revocation is hard.
- Verify signature, `exp`, `iss`, `aud`; pin the algorithm.

### OAUTH 2.1 (still an IETF draft in 2026, but it IS current best practice)
It consolidates OAuth 2.0 plus its security fixes (RFC 9700, Jan 2025):
- Authorization code flow with PKCE for ALL clients
- Implicit flow and password grant removed
- Exact redirect URI matching; refresh tokens rotated or sender-bound

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User's browser
    participant App as Your app
    participant AS as Auth server
    App->>U: Redirect to AS with code_challenge (PKCE)
    U->>AS: Log in + consent
    AS->>U: Redirect back with ?code=...
    U->>App: code
    App->>AS: code + code_verifier
    AS->>App: access token (+ refresh token)
```
Don't build your own authorization server: use a library or a provider (Keycloak, Auth0, Cognito, Zitadel).

### SOURCES
- https://oauth.net/2.1/
- https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9700
- https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/REST_Security_Cheat_Sheet.html
- https://openid.net/developers/how-connect-works/

nodes.title: Rate limiting & throttling
nodes.content:
### WHY
Stop brute force, scraping and abuse; protect expensive endpoints; share capacity fairly between customers.

### THE ALGORITHMS
| Algorithm | How | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| Fixed window | Count per minute; reset at :00 | Simple; allows 2x bursts at window edges |
| Sliding window | Weighted count over the last 60 s | Smoother; slightly more work |
| Token bucket | Bucket refills N tokens/sec; each request takes one | Allows short bursts, enforces average. Most common |
| Leaky bucket | Requests drain at a constant rate | Very smooth output; queues or drops bursts |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    R["Request"] --> T{"Tokens left in bucket?"}
    T -->|yes| OK["Take 1 token -> handle request"]
    T -->|no| NO["429 Too Many Requests + Retry-After"]
    REFILL["Refill: +10 tokens/sec up to max 50"] -.-> T
```

### SIMPLE FIXED WINDOW IN PHP + MYSQL
```php
$key = 'login:' . $_SERVER['REMOTE_ADDR'];
$window = intdiv(time(), 60); // current minute
$pdo->prepare('INSERT INTO rate_limits (rl_key, rl_window, hits) VALUES (?, ?, 1)
               ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE hits = hits + 1')->execute([$key, $window]);
$stmt = $pdo->prepare('SELECT hits FROM rate_limits WHERE rl_key = ? AND rl_window = ?');
$stmt->execute([$key, $window]);
if ($stmt->fetchColumn() > 10) {
    http_response_code(429);
    header('Retry-After: 60');
    exit;
}
```
(Primary key on `(rl_key, rl_window)`; delete old windows with a cron job. Redis `INCR` + `EXPIRE` does the same faster.)

### TELL CLIENTS THE RULES
- Always `429` + `Retry-After`.
- IETF draft `RateLimit-Policy` / `RateLimit` headers (draft-11, May 2026) standardise "you have N requests left". Many APIs still use `X-RateLimit-Remaining`.

### CLIENT SIDE: BACK OFF
Retry with exponential backoff + jitter: wait 1 s, 2 s, 4 s, 8 s... each with a random +-50%, so thousands of clients don't retry in sync.

### WHERE TO ENFORCE
At the edge (Cloudflare, API gateway, nginx `limit_req`) for raw floods; in the app for per-user and per-endpoint business rules.

### SOURCES
- https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-httpapi-ratelimit-headers/
- https://blog.cloudflare.com/counting-things-a-lot-of-different-things/
- https://aws.amazon.com/builders-library/timeouts-retries-and-backoff-with-jitter/

nodes.title: Caching & CDNs
nodes.content:
### CACHING LAYERS (closest to the user wins)
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    B["Browser cache"] --> CDN["CDN edge"] --> RP["Reverse proxy"] --> APP["App cache (Redis/APCu)"] --> DB[("DB buffer pool")]
```

### HTTP CACHE-CONTROL CHEAT SHEET
| Directive | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `max-age=31536000, immutable` | Cache 1 year, never revalidate (for hashed filenames like `app.3f9a1c.js`) |
| `no-cache` | May store, but must revalidate every time (ETag check) |
| `no-store` | Never store (sensitive pages) |
| `private` | Browser only, not shared caches/CDNs (per-user pages) |
| `s-maxage=60` | How long shared caches (CDN) may keep it |
| `stale-while-revalidate=30` | Serve stale for 30 s while fetching fresh in background |

### VALIDATION: ETAG + 304
Server sends `ETag: "v5"`. Next time the browser sends `If-None-Match: "v5"`; if unchanged, the server replies `304 Not Modified` with no body. Saves bandwidth, not round trips.

### CACHE BUSTING
Long cache for static files + a changing URL when content changes: `style.css?v=12` or build-hashed names. Then HTML itself gets `no-cache`.

### APPLICATION CACHES
- APCu: per-server in-memory PHP cache (fast, not shared between servers)
- Redis/Valkey: shared cache for many app servers (see "Scaling a database" for cache-aside)
- Cache computed results (rendered fragments, API responses), not just DB rows

### CDNs
Copies of your static files (and optionally pages) on servers near users: Cloudflare, CloudFront, Fastly, Bunny. They also absorb DDoS traffic and terminate TLS.

### "THERE ARE ONLY TWO HARD THINGS..."
Cache invalidation is genuinely hard. Prefer short TTLs and versioned URLs over clever invalidation logic. Never cache responses containing one user's private data in a shared cache.

### SOURCES
- https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Guides/Caching
- https://web.dev/articles/http-cache
- https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9111

nodes.title: Load balancing
nodes.content:
### WHAT A LOAD BALANCER DOES
Spreads incoming requests over several servers so you can (1) handle more traffic and (2) survive a server dying. Also: TLS termination, health checks, zero-downtime deploys (drain one server at a time).

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    C["Clients"] --> LB["Load balancer (TLS ends here)"]
    LB -->|healthy| S1["App 1"]
    LB -->|healthy| S2["App 2"]
    LB -.->|"failed health check: gets no traffic"| S3["App 3"]
    S1 --> SH[("Shared: DB, Redis sessions, S3 files")]
    S2 --> SH
```

### LAYER 4 VS LAYER 7
- L4 (TCP/UDP): forwards connections by IP/port without looking inside. Very fast. (AWS NLB, HAProxy TCP mode)
- L7 (HTTP): reads the request, so it can route by path/host/header (`/api` -> API servers), add headers, do retries. (nginx, HAProxy, Apache mod_proxy_balancer, AWS ALB, Cloudflare)

### ALGORITHMS
- Round robin: take turns. Great when servers and requests are similar.
- Weighted round robin: bigger servers get more.
- Least connections: send to the least busy. Good default when request times vary.
- IP hash / consistent hashing: same client or key goes to the same server (keeps caches warm; minimal reshuffling when servers change).

### HEALTH CHECKS
- Shallow: is the port open? Misses "PHP is up but can't reach the DB".
- Deep: `GET /health.php` checks DB/Redis and returns 200 or 503. Keep it cheap and don't let one flaky dependency eject every server.

### MAKE APP SERVERS STATELESS
If sessions live in local files, a user bounced to another server is logged out. Options: "sticky sessions" (a band-aid) or, better, sessions in Redis/DB and uploads in shared storage (S3). Then any server can handle any request and scaling is just "add another".

### APACHE AS A LOAD BALANCER
```apache
<Proxy "balancer://app">
    BalancerMember "http://10.0.0.11:8080"
    BalancerMember "http://10.0.0.12:8080"
    ProxySet lbmethod=bybusyness
</Proxy>
ProxyPass        "/" "balancer://app/"
ProxyPassReverse "/" "balancer://app/"
```
(Needs `mod_proxy`, `mod_proxy_balancer`, `mod_lbmethod_bybusyness`.)

### GLOBAL LOAD BALANCING
Across regions: DNS-based (Route 53 latency routing) or anycast (Cloudflare) sends users to the nearest healthy region.

### SOURCES
- https://httpd.apache.org/docs/2.4/mod/mod_proxy_balancer.html
- https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/load_balancing.html
- https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/userguide/how-elastic-load-balancing-works.html
- https://samwho.dev/load-balancing/ (excellent interactive explainer)

nodes.title: Reverse proxies, API gateways & service meshes
nodes.content:
### FOUR THINGS THAT SIT IN FRONT OF YOUR CODE
| Thing | Job | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| Reverse proxy | Accepts requests for your servers: TLS, compression, static files, forwarding | nginx, Apache, Caddy, Traefik |
| Load balancer | A reverse proxy that spreads traffic over many servers | HAProxy, AWS ALB/NLB |
| API gateway | Load balancer + API concerns: auth, API keys, rate limits, quotas, request validation, analytics | AWS API Gateway, Kong, Tyk, Apigee |
| Service mesh | Sidecar proxies between internal services: mTLS, retries, tracing | Istio, Linkerd |
In practice the lines blur: nginx can do most of it.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    C["Clients"] --> GW["API gateway: auth, rate limit, routing"]
    GW -->|"/users"| US["Users service"]
    GW -->|"/orders"| OS["Orders service"]
    GW -->|"/search"| SS["Search service"]
```

### WHY A GATEWAY
- One place for cross-cutting concerns, so every service doesn't reimplement auth and rate limiting
- Clients see one stable URL even if services move or split
- Can translate protocols (REST outside, gRPC inside)

### THE COSTS
Another hop of latency, another thing to configure and monitor, and a single point of failure if not redundant. For a monolith (one PHP app) a reverse proxy is all you need; gateways pay off with many services or public APIs with paying customers.

### SERVERLESS PAIRING
AWS API Gateway + Lambda is a common "no servers" stack: the gateway handles HTTP, auth and throttling, Lambda runs your code per request.

### AI GATEWAYS (2026 trend)
The same idea for LLM calls: one proxy in front of several AI providers that handles API keys, rate limits, cost tracking, caching and fallbacks (Cloudflare AI Gateway, LiteLLM, Kong AI Gateway).

### SOURCES
- https://microservices.io/patterns/apigateway.html
- https://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_proxy_module.html
- https://docs.aws.amazon.com/apigateway/latest/developerguide/welcome.html

nodes.title: Containers explained
nodes.content:
### THE PROBLEM
"Works on my machine": different PHP versions, missing extensions, other library versions on the server. A container packages your app WITH its runtime and dependencies so it runs the same everywhere.

### THE VOCABULARY
- Image: a read-only template (OS files + PHP + your code), built in layers. Like a class.
- Container: a running instance of an image. Like an object. Throw-away by design.
- Dockerfile: the recipe to build an image.
- Registry: where images are stored and shared (Docker Hub, GitHub Container Registry, AWS ECR).
- OCI: the open standard; images built with Docker also run on Podman, containerd, Kubernetes.

### CONTAINER VS VIRTUAL MACHINE
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph VM ["Virtual machines"]
        A1["App A"] --> G1["Guest OS (full kernel)"]
        A2["App B"] --> G2["Guest OS (full kernel)"]
        G1 --> HV["Hypervisor"]
        G2 --> HV
    end
    subgraph CT ["Containers"]
        C1["App A + libs"] --> K["Shared host kernel + container runtime"]
        C2["App B + libs"] --> K
    end
```
Containers share the host's kernel: they start in milliseconds and use far less memory than VMs, but isolation is weaker (a kernel bug affects all).

### FIRST COMMANDS
```bash
docker run -d --name web -p 8080:80 php:8.4-apache  # start a container
docker ps                    # list running containers
docker logs -f web           # follow its output
docker exec -it web bash     # shell inside it
docker stop web && docker rm web
docker images                # list local images
```

### DOCKER VS PODMAN
Podman runs the same images without a background daemon and rootless by default; `alias docker=podman` mostly works. Docker Desktop (Mac/Windows) runs a small Linux VM for you; on Linux, Docker Engine runs natively.

### DO YOU NEED IT?
For one PHP app on your own server, Apache directly is simpler. Containers shine when you deploy to the cloud, run several apps with different versions, or want identical dev/prod environments.

### SOURCES
- https://docs.docker.com/get-started/docker-overview/
- https://opencontainers.org/
- https://podman.io/

nodes.title: Writing a good Dockerfile
nodes.content:
### A PHP + APACHE EXAMPLE
```dockerfile
# Stage 1: install PHP dependencies with Composer (this stage is thrown away)
FROM composer:2 AS deps
WORKDIR /app
COPY composer.json composer.lock ./
RUN composer install --no-dev --prefer-dist --no-interaction

# Stage 2: the image that actually runs
FROM php:8.4-apache
RUN docker-php-ext-install pdo_mysql \
 && a2enmod rewrite headers
COPY --from=deps /app/vendor /var/www/html/vendor
COPY . /var/www/html/
RUN chown -R www-data:www-data /var/www/html
HEALTHCHECK CMD curl -fs http://localhost/health.php || exit 1
```

### THE BEST PRACTICES (Docker's official guide)
- Multi-stage builds: build tools stay in earlier stages; the final image holds only what runs.
- Order for caching: copy dependency manifests and install BEFORE copying source, so code edits don't reinstall everything.
- `.dockerignore`: exclude `.git`, `node_modules`, `.env`, logs, backups (smaller, faster, no leaked secrets).
- Pin base images: a version tag at least (`php:8.4-apache`), a digest for full reproducibility (`@sha256:...`), and let Dependabot/Renovate bump it.
- `apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends ...` in ONE `RUN`, then `rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*`.
- Run as a non-root `USER` when the process allows it.
- `COPY`, not `ADD`, unless you need ADD's URL download or tar extraction.
- Exec form for commands: `CMD ["php", "worker.php"]` (signals reach your process, so containers stop cleanly).
- Rebuild regularly with `docker build --pull` to pick up base-image security patches.
- One concern per container (web server, DB and worker in separate containers).

### SECRETS DURING BUILDS
Never `COPY .env` or pass tokens as `ARG`: they stay in image layers forever. Use BuildKit secrets: `RUN --mount=type=secret,id=composer_auth ...`.

### BUILD AND RUN
```bash
docker build -t myapp:1.0 .
docker run -d -p 8080:80 myapp:1.0
```

### SOURCES
- https://docs.docker.com/build/building/best-practices/
- https://docs.docker.com/build/building/multi-stage/
- https://hub.docker.com/_/php

nodes.title: Docker Compose for local development
nodes.content:
### ONE FILE, WHOLE STACK
`compose.yaml` describes several containers that work together. `docker compose up` starts them all.
```yaml
services:
  web:
    build: .
    ports:
      - "8080:80"
    environment:
      DB_HOST: db          # service names work as hostnames
      DB_NAME: app
    volumes:
      - ./src:/var/www/html  # live code editing in dev
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy  # wait until the DB really accepts connections

  db:
    image: mariadb:11.8
    environment:
      MARIADB_DATABASE: app
      MARIADB_USER: app
      MARIADB_PASSWORD: secret
      MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD: rootsecret
    volumes:
      - dbdata:/var/lib/mysql   # data survives container rebuilds
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "healthcheck.sh", "--connect", "--innodb_initialized"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 10

volumes:
  dbdata:
```

### DAILY COMMANDS
```bash
docker compose up -d          # start in the background
docker compose logs -f web    # follow logs
docker compose exec db mariadb -u app -p app   # SQL shell
docker compose down           # stop (keeps volumes)
docker compose down -v        # stop AND delete data volumes
```

### GOOD TO KNOW
- Plain `depends_on` only waits for the container to START; add a healthcheck + `condition: service_healthy` to wait for readiness.
- The old `version:` key and the `docker-compose` (hyphen) command are obsolete; it's `docker compose` now.
- `docker compose watch` with a `develop.watch` section syncs file changes or rebuilds automatically: an alternative to bind mounts.
- Keep real secrets in a `.env` file that's in `.gitignore`; Compose reads it automatically.
- Profiles (`profiles: [tools]`) for optional services like phpMyAdmin or Adminer.

### SOURCES
- https://docs.docker.com/compose/gettingstarted/
- https://docs.docker.com/compose/how-tos/startup-order/
- https://docs.docker.com/compose/how-tos/file-watch/
- https://hub.docker.com/_/mariadb

nodes.title: Volumes, networks & data
nodes.content:
### CONTAINERS FORGET EVERYTHING
Anything written inside a container is lost when it's removed. Persistent data must live outside it.

### THREE KINDS OF STORAGE
| Kind | Syntax | Use for |
|---|---|---|
| Named volume | `dbdata:/var/lib/mysql` | Database files, uploads. Managed by Docker |
| Bind mount | `./src:/var/www/html` | Live source code in development, config files |
| tmpfs | `tmpfs: /tmp` | Scratch data in RAM |
Back up a named volume by running a throwaway container that tars it, or (better for DBs) with `mariadb-dump` from inside the DB container.

### NETWORKING
- Compose creates a private network per project; containers reach each other by service name (`db:3306`).
- Only what you publish with `ports:` is reachable from outside.
- Publish to localhost only when outsiders don't need it: `"127.0.0.1:3306:3306"`.

### THE UFW GOTCHA (important on Ubuntu/Debian)
Docker writes its own iptables rules, so ports you publish with `-p 3306:3306` are reachable from the network EVEN IF UFW denies them. Bind to `127.0.0.1`, don't publish internal services at all, or use the `DOCKER-USER` iptables chain.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    NET["LAN / internet"] -->|"published 8080"| WEB["web container"]
    WEB -->|"internal network: db:3306"| DB["db container"]
    NET -.->|"blocked: port not published"| DB
    DB --- VOL[("named volume dbdata")]
```

### FILE PERMISSIONS
A bind-mounted folder keeps host ownership; if the container runs as `www-data` (UID 33) it may not be able to write. Match UIDs, or set the container user to your host UID in development.

### SOURCES
- https://docs.docker.com/engine/storage/volumes/
- https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/
- https://docs.docker.com/engine/network/packet-filtering-firewalls/

nodes.title: Container security
nodes.content:
### THE BASICS
- Run as non-root (`USER` in the Dockerfile). If the app is compromised, the attacker isn't root inside the container.
- Never `--privileged`, never mount `/var/run/docker.sock` into a container (it's root on the host).
- Minimal base images: fewer packages = fewer vulnerabilities. Options: `-slim` Debian images, Alpine, distroless.
- No secrets baked into images; inject them at runtime (env vars, Docker/Kubernetes secrets).
- Read-only filesystem where possible (`read_only: true` + a tmpfs for `/tmp`), drop Linux capabilities (`cap_drop: [ALL]`).
- Set memory/CPU limits so one container can't starve the host.

### DOCKER HARDENED IMAGES (free since December 2025)
Docker made its hardened, minimal, distroless-style base images free and open source: 1,000+ images (Debian/Alpine bases, language runtimes, databases) with near-zero known CVEs, signed SBOMs and SLSA Level 3 provenance. Worth trying as base images.

### SCAN AND UPDATE
- Scan images for known CVEs: `docker scout cves myapp:1.0`, Trivy, Grype. Run it in CI.
- Rebuild on a schedule (weekly) with `--pull`: a scan is useless if nobody rebuilds.
- SBOM (software bill of materials): the list of everything inside the image. `docker buildx build --sbom=true --provenance=true`.

### SUPPLY CHAIN
- Use official / verified images; pin by digest in production.
- Sign images (Sigstore cosign, Docker Content Trust) and verify before deploying.

### ROOTLESS MODE
Run the Docker daemon itself as a normal user (or use Podman), so even a container escape lands as an unprivileged user.

### SOURCES
- https://docs.docker.com/engine/security/
- https://www.docker.com/blog/hardened-images-free-now-what/
- https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Docker_Security_Cheat_Sheet.html
- https://docs.docker.com/scout/

nodes.title: Orchestration, Kubernetes & Docker in 2026
nodes.content:
### WHEN ONE HOST ISN'T ENOUGH
An orchestrator runs containers across many machines: restarts crashed ones, scales replicas, rolls out new versions, routes traffic.

### KUBERNETES IN SIX WORDS
- Pod: one or more containers scheduled together
- Deployment: "keep 3 replicas of this pod, update them gradually"
- Service: a stable internal address for a set of pods
- Gateway API / Ingress: route outside HTTP traffic to services
- ConfigMap / Secret: configuration injected into pods
- Namespace: a folder for resources
You describe the desired state in YAML; Kubernetes keeps reality matching it.

### KUBERNETES IN 2026
- v1.36 "Haru" (April 2026): stronger user-namespace isolation, Kubelet API hardening, better scheduling for AI/GPU workloads.
- The popular ingress-nginx controller was retired (March 2026): new setups use the Gateway API.
- Managed offerings (EKS, GKE, AKS) are the norm; few teams run the control plane themselves.

### SIMPLER OPTIONS (often the better choice)
- Docker Compose on one VM: fine for most small products
- Managed containers: AWS ECS/Fargate, Google Cloud Run, Azure Container Apps, Fly.io
- Self-hosted PaaS: Coolify, Dokku, Kamal (deploy containers to your own servers over SSH)
Kubernetes is powerful but a full-time skill; adopt it when you have many services and a team to run it.

### WHAT'S NEW IN DOCKER (2025-2026)
- Docker Hardened Images free and open source (Dec 2025)
- Docker Model Runner: pull and run LLMs locally with an OpenAI-compatible API (`docker model run ...`)
- MCP Catalog & Toolkit: hundreds of MCP servers for AI assistants, run as isolated containers behind a gateway
- Docker Sandboxes: disposable microVMs to let AI coding agents run code safely
- Compose is now v5; Docker Desktop ships every two weeks

### SOURCES
- https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/
- https://kubernetes.io/blog/2025/11/11/ingress-nginx-retirement/
- https://gateway-api.sigs.k8s.io/
- https://www.docker.com/blog/

nodes.title: Start here: how AWS is organised
nodes.content:
### THE GLOBAL LAYOUT
- Region: a geographic area (eu-west-1 Ireland, us-east-1 Virginia). Pick one near your users; prices and services differ slightly.
- Availability Zone (AZ): one or more separate data centres inside a region. Spread across 2+ AZs to survive one failing.
- Edge locations: hundreds of CDN points for CloudFront and Route 53.

### ACCOUNTS
An AWS account is a security and billing boundary. Real setups use AWS Organizations: separate accounts for dev, prod, and logging/security, with central billing.

### THE SHARED RESPONSIBILITY MODEL
AWS secures the cloud (hardware, data centres, the services); YOU secure what you put in it (IAM permissions, OS patches on EC2, open security groups, public S3 buckets, your code).

### THE ~15 SERVICES MOST APPS USE
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph EDGE ["Edge"]
        R53["Route 53 (DNS)"]
        CF["CloudFront (CDN)"]
    end
    subgraph APP ["Compute"]
        ALB["ALB (load balancer)"]
        EC2["EC2 / ECS / Lambda"]
    end
    subgraph DATA ["Data"]
        RDS[("RDS / Aurora")]
        S3[("S3")]
        DDB[("DynamoDB")]
    end
    R53 --> CF --> ALB --> EC2
    EC2 --> RDS
    EC2 --> S3
    EC2 --> DDB
```
Plus: IAM (permissions), VPC (network), CloudWatch (logs & metrics), Secrets Manager, SQS (queues), SES (email), ACM (TLS certificates).

### HOW YOU TALK TO AWS
Web console (learning), AWS CLI (scripts), SDKs (your code, e.g. `aws/aws-sdk-php`), and Infrastructure as Code (CloudFormation, CDK, Terraform/OpenTofu) for anything real.

### THE FREE TIER CHANGED (July 15, 2025)
