nodes.title: IAM: identities & permissions
nodes.content:
### THE PIECES
- Root user: the account's email login. Can do anything. Use it almost never.
- IAM users / IAM Identity Center users: people.
- Roles: identities that are ASSUMED, giving temporary credentials. Used by EC2 instances, Lambda functions, CI pipelines, and people via Identity Center.
- Policies: JSON documents listing allowed (or denied) actions on resources.

### A POLICY
```json
{
  "Version": "2012-10-17",
  "Statement": [{
    "Effect": "Allow",
    "Action": ["s3:GetObject", "s3:PutObject"],
    "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::myapp-uploads/*"
  }]
}
```
Evaluation: everything is denied by default; an Allow grants; an explicit Deny anywhere always wins.

### AWS'S BEST PRACTICES
- Root: MFA on (passkey or security key), no access keys, locked away.
- Humans: IAM Identity Center with temporary credentials, not long-lived IAM user keys.
- Workloads: roles (EC2 instance profile, Lambda execution role, ECS task role). The SDK picks up credentials automatically; no keys in code or `.env`.
- CI/CD: GitHub Actions assumes a role via OIDC, so no AWS keys stored in GitHub.
- Least privilege: start from AWS managed policies, then tighten with IAM Access Analyzer (it can generate a policy from actual usage).
- Remove unused users, roles and keys; rotate any unavoidable access keys.

### NEW: IAM POLICY AUTOPILOT (re:Invent 2025)
An open-source MCP server that reads your code and generates the IAM policy it needs, so AI coding assistants can propose least-privilege policies.

### COMMON MISTAKES
- `"Action": "*", "Resource": "*"` on an app role
- Access keys committed to git (bots scan GitHub within minutes)
- One shared admin user for the whole team

### SOURCES
- https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/best-practices.html
- https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/root-user-best-practices.html
- https://docs.github.com/en/actions/deployment/security-hardening-your-deployments/configuring-openid-connect-in-amazon-web-services

nodes.title: Compute: EC2, Lambda, ECS/Fargate, Lightsail
nodes.content:
### THE OPTIONS
| Service | What you manage | Billing | Best for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lightsail | A simple VPS (fixed monthly price, includes traffic) | Monthly | Small PHP sites, learning |
| EC2 | Virtual machines: OS, patches, scaling | Per second | Full control, long-running servers |
| ECS on Fargate | Containers; no servers to patch | Per vCPU/GB-second | Dockerised apps |
| EKS | Kubernetes clusters | Cluster + nodes | Teams already on Kubernetes |
| Lambda | Just functions; AWS runs them on events | Per request + duration | APIs with spiky traffic, background jobs, glue |

### EC2 ESSENTIALS
- Instance types: `t4g`/`t3` (burstable, cheap), `m` (general), `c` (CPU), `r` (memory). The `g` suffix = Graviton (ARM): typically ~20% cheaper for the same work; PHP runs fine on it. Graviton5 was announced at re:Invent 2025.
- AMI = the disk image you boot from. EBS = the attached disk.
- Auto Scaling Group: keeps N instances running, replaces unhealthy ones, scales on CPU or requests.
- Security group = a stateful firewall per instance (allow 443 from the load balancer only, 22 from your IP only, or use SSM Session Manager and open no SSH port at all).

### LAMBDA ESSENTIALS
- Triggers: API Gateway / function URLs, S3 uploads, SQS messages, schedules.
- Limits: max 15 minutes per run; "cold starts" add latency to the first request.
- PHP on Lambda: the Bref project.
- New at re:Invent 2025: Lambda Managed Instances (run functions on EC2 capacity and pricing) and Lambda Durable Functions (multi-step workflows that can wait hours or days without paying for idle time).

### HOW TO CHOOSE
Steady traffic and a classic PHP app: Lightsail or EC2. Containers: Fargate. Spiky or event-driven: Lambda. Don't adopt Kubernetes to run one app.

- https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/welcome.html

nodes.title: Storage & databases: S3, EBS, RDS, DynamoDB
nodes.content:
### S3: OBJECT STORAGE
Unlimited files ("objects") in "buckets", accessed over HTTP. Durability 11 nines.
- Uploads, backups, static sites, data lakes.
- Block Public Access is on by default: keep it on; serve public files through CloudFront.
- Presigned URLs: let a browser upload/download one file directly for a few minutes without exposing credentials.
- Storage classes: Standard -> Intelligent-Tiering -> Glacier (cheap, slow retrieval). Lifecycle rules move/delete old objects.
- Turn on versioning for anything important (protects against accidental deletes).
- New: S3 Vectors (GA Dec 2025) stores and queries embeddings cheaply for AI search.

### BLOCK AND FILE STORAGE
- EBS: a virtual disk attached to one EC2 instance. Snapshot it for backups.
- EFS: a shared network file system (NFS) many instances mount at once.

### RELATIONAL: RDS & AURORA
- RDS runs MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL (and others) for you: patches, automated backups, point-in-time restore, read replicas.
- Multi-AZ: a standby copy in another AZ with automatic failover.
- Aurora: AWS's MySQL/PostgreSQL-compatible engine; faster failover, storage grows automatically; Aurora Serverless v2 scales capacity up and down; Aurora DSQL is a distributed, serverless option.
- Your PHP connects exactly as before (PDO + hostname); keep the DB in a private subnet.

### NOSQL: DYNAMODB
Key-value/document database, single-digit-millisecond at any scale, serverless pricing. Rule: design tables around your exact queries (partition key + sort key). Ad-hoc queries and joins are painful.

### CACHING: ELASTICACHE
Managed Redis/Valkey/Memcached for sessions and caches.

### PICKING
Default for a PHP app: RDS MariaDB/MySQL or PostgreSQL + S3 for files. DynamoDB when access patterns are simple and scale is huge.

### SOURCES
- https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/Welcome.html
- https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/Welcome.html
- https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/bp-general-nosql-design.html

nodes.title: Networking: VPC, ALB, Route 53, CloudFront
nodes.content:
### VPC: YOUR PRIVATE NETWORK
A Virtual Private Cloud is an isolated network (e.g. `10.0.0.0/16`) in one region, split into subnets per AZ.
- Public subnet: has a route to the Internet Gateway. Load balancers live here.
- Private subnet: no direct inbound internet. App servers and databases live here.
- NAT Gateway: lets private servers make OUTBOUND calls (updates, APIs). Note: ~$30+/month each plus data charges: a classic surprise bill.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    INT["Internet"] --> R53["Route 53"] --> CF["CloudFront"]
    CF --> ALB
    subgraph VPC ["VPC 10.0.0.0/16"]
        subgraph PUB ["Public subnets (2 AZs)"]
            ALB["Application Load Balancer"]
            NAT["NAT gateway"]
        end
        subgraph PRIV ["Private subnets (2 AZs)"]
            APP["App servers / Fargate tasks"]
            DB[("RDS Multi-AZ")]
        end
    end
    ALB --> APP --> DB
    APP -->|outbound only| NAT
```

### FIREWALLS
- Security groups: stateful, attached to instances/load balancers/DBs. Reference each other: "DB allows 3306 only from the app's security group". This is the main tool.
- Network ACLs: stateless, per subnet. Usually left at defaults.

### LOAD BALANCERS
- ALB (Layer 7): HTTP routing by host/path, TLS with free ACM certificates, health checks.
- NLB (Layer 4): TCP/UDP, ultra-low latency, static IPs.

### DNS AND CDN
- Route 53: DNS, plus health-checked failover and latency-based routing between regions.
- CloudFront: CDN in front of S3 (static sites, uploads) and your ALB; TLS, caching, WAF rules.

### COST TRAPS
NAT gateways, cross-AZ and outbound data transfer, and public IPv4 addresses (charged per hour since 2024). Use VPC endpoints for S3/DynamoDB traffic from private subnets.

### SOURCES
- https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/what-is-amazon-vpc.html
- https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/userguide/vpc-security-groups.html
- https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticloadbalancing/latest/application/introduction.html

nodes.title: Deploying a PHP app on AWS
nodes.content:
### FIVE PATHS, SIMPLEST FIRST
1. Lightsail LAMP instance: a VPS with Apache + PHP preinstalled. Copy your app, point a domain at it. Closest to a classic single-server setup.
2. EC2 + RDS: your own VM in a VPC, with a managed database. Add an ALB + Auto Scaling later.
3. Elastic Beanstalk (PHP platform): upload a zip; it creates EC2, load balancer and scaling for you.
4. ECS Fargate + ALB + RDS: run your Docker image without managing servers.
5. Lambda via Bref: serverless PHP; pay per request.

### A SOLID "PATH 2" CHECKLIST
- RDS (MariaDB/MySQL) in private subnets, Multi-AZ for production, automated backups on.
- EC2 in a private subnet behind an ALB; HTTPS certificate from ACM on the ALB.
- DB password in Secrets Manager or SSM Parameter Store; the instance role may read only that secret.
- Sessions in the database or ElastiCache (so you can add a second server), uploads in S3.
- Logs to CloudWatch (CloudWatch agent); alarms on 5xx errors and high CPU.
- SSM Session Manager instead of an open SSH port.

### INFRASTRUCTURE AS CODE
Click-ops in the console is fine for learning, but write real environments as code so they're reviewable and repeatable: AWS CDK (TypeScript/Python), CloudFormation (YAML), or Terraform/OpenTofu (multi-cloud).

### CI/CD
GitHub Actions: on push to `main` -> run tests -> build the image or zip -> deploy. Authenticate with OIDC role assumption (no stored AWS keys).

### STATIC FRONTENDS
A Vue SPA build = static files: put them in S3 behind CloudFront (or AWS Amplify Hosting) and call your API from there.

### SOURCES
- https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lightsail/
- https://docs.aws.amazon.com/elasticbeanstalk/latest/dg/create_deploy_PHP_eb.html
- https://bref.sh/docs/
- https://docs.aws.amazon.com/cdk/v2/guide/home.html

nodes.title: Cost control & the Well-Architected Framework
nodes.content:
### DAY-ONE COST HYGIENE
- AWS Budgets: email alerts at 50%/80%/100% of a monthly amount.
- Cost Explorer: see spend by service; enable Cost Anomaly Detection.
- Tag everything (`project=budgetbee`, `env=prod`) to see what each app costs.
- Delete experiments: stopped EC2 instances still pay for their EBS disks and Elastic IPs.

### WHERE SURPRISE BILLS COME FROM
NAT gateways, data transfer out to the internet and between AZs, public IPv4 addresses, oversized RDS instances, CloudWatch Logs ingestion, forgotten load balancers, idle EKS clusters.

### PAYING LESS
- Right-size: most instances are oversized; check CPU/memory graphs.
- Graviton (ARM) instances: usually cheaper per unit of work.
- Savings Plans / Reserved Instances: 1-3 year commitment for steady workloads (up to ~70% off). Database Savings Plans arrived at re:Invent 2025.
- Spot instances: up to ~90% off for interruptible work (batch jobs, CI).
- Serverless (Lambda, Fargate, Aurora Serverless) for spiky or low traffic.
- S3 lifecycle rules and Intelligent-Tiering.

### THE WELL-ARCHITECTED FRAMEWORK: SIX PILLARS
1. Operational excellence: automate deploys, monitor, learn from incidents
2. Security: least privilege, encryption, traceability
3. Reliability: multi-AZ, backups, recover automatically, test failure
4. Performance efficiency: right resource types, measure, use managed services
5. Cost optimisation: pay only for what you need, measure spend
6. Sustainability: use less energy (efficient code, right-sizing, Graviton)
The free Well-Architected Tool asks questions per pillar and lists risks; AWS refreshed the best practices in 2025. The same questions are a great system-design interview checklist.

nodes.title: Start here: the frontend & mobile map
nodes.content:
### FOUR TOPICS, ONE GOAL
Ship interfaces that work well on the device people actually hold: usually a mid-range phone on a so-so connection.
1. Mobile-first fundamentals: layout, touch, performance
2. New concepts in web development: what the platform can do natively in 2026
3. Hybrid mobile development: one codebase, app-store apps
4. Graph & chart libraries: showing data

### HOW THEY CONNECT
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    W["Your web app (Vue + PHP API)"] --> R["Responsive, mobile-first UI"]
    R --> P["PWA: installable, offline, push"]
    P --> C["Capacitor: same code in App Store / Play Store"]
    W -.->|"or rewrite UI"| N["React Native / Flutter / KMP: native-feeling apps"]
```
A web developer's natural path: make the web app great on phones, then make it installable, then wrap it for the stores if needed. A separate native-UI framework is the bigger leap, worth it when performance or platform feel really matter (or for the job market).

### THE 2026 THEME: THE PLATFORM CAUGHT UP
Many things that needed JavaScript libraries (tooltips, modals, accordions, carousels, page transitions, date handling) are now built into browsers. Less JS = faster on phones and fewer dependencies to keep updated.

nodes.title: What mobile-first really means
nodes.content:
### THE IDEA
Design and build for the smallest screen and the hardest conditions FIRST (small screen, touch, slow CPU, flaky network), then enhance for larger screens. It's a content-priority exercise: if it doesn't fit on a phone, is it really important?

### WHY IT'S THE DEFAULT
- Roughly 60% of global web traffic is mobile (StatCounter).
- Google indexes the mobile version of your site (mobile-first indexing has applied to all sites since 2024).
- Starting small is easier than cramming a desktop design into a phone later.

### IN CSS: BASE STYLES = MOBILE, MEDIA QUERIES ADD
```css
/* Mobile: one column, by default */
.layout { display: grid; gap: 1rem; }

/* Wider screens: add a sidebar */
@media (min-width: 48rem) {
  .layout { grid-template-columns: 16rem 1fr; }
}
```
Use `min-width` queries (mobile-first), not `max-width` overrides (desktop-first).

### PATTERNS THAT WORK
- One pane at a time on phones: list -> detail with a back button; panes side by side only on wide screens
- Bottom navigation or a simple menu button instead of wide nav bars
- Sticky primary action ("Save") within thumb reach
- Progressive disclosure: hide secondary options behind "More"
- Tables: let them scroll horizontally inside a wrapper, or turn rows into cards

### PROGRESSIVE ENHANCEMENT
The core task (read, submit a form) should work with plain HTML; JavaScript enhances. Then a failed script load or old device still gets a usable page.

### TEST LIKE A USER
Browser dev tools' device mode for layout, then a REAL mid-range Android phone for performance and touch. Rotate it. Try one-handed use.

### SOURCES
- https://web.dev/learn/design
- https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/mobile/mobile-sites-mobile-first-indexing
- https://gs.statcounter.com/platform-market-share/desktop-mobile-tablet

nodes.title: The responsive layout toolkit
nodes.content: ### 1. THE VIEWPORT TAG (always) ```html ``` Never add `user-scalable=no`: blocking zoom is an accessibility failure. ### 2. FLUID SIZES - `rem` for type and spacing; `%`, `fr` and `minmax()` for layout - Fluid type with `clamp()`: `font-size: clamp(1rem, 0.9rem + 0.5vw, 1.25rem);` ### 3. GRID THAT ADAPTS WITHOUT MEDIA QUERIES ```css .cards { display: grid; gap: 1rem; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(16rem, 1fr)); } ``` ### 4. CONTAINER QUERIES (widely available since 2025) Components respond to THEIR container's width, not the window's, so the same card works in a sidebar and in the main area: ```css .card-wrap { container-type: inline-size; } @container (min-width: 30rem) { .card { display: flex; } } ``` Container STYLE queries (`@container style(--theme: dark)`) became Baseline in 2026. ### 5. VIEWPORT UNITS THAT RESPECT MOBILE BROWSER BARS `100vh` is taller than the visible area on phones (the address bar). Use: - `100dvh`: dynamic, follows the bars as they show/hide - `100svh`: smallest (bars visible), `100lvh`: largest ### 6. RESPONSIVE IMAGES ```html ``` `width`/`height` prevent layout shift; `aspect-ratio` does the same in CSS. ### 7. NOTCHES AND HOME BARS `padding-bottom: env(safe-area-inset-bottom);` with `viewport-fit=cover` in the viewport tag. ### BREAKPOINTS Pick them where YOUR content breaks, not for specific devices. Two or three are usually enough. ### SOURCES - https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/CSS_containment/Container_queries - https://web.dev/learn/design/responsive-images - https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/CSS/length#relative_length_units_based_on_viewport

nodes.title: Touch, forms & accessibility on phones
nodes.content:
### TOUCH TARGETS
- WCAG 2.2 success criterion 2.5.8 (level AA): targets at least 24x24 CSS pixels (or enough spacing around them).
- Platform guidance is more generous: Apple 44x44 pt, Material 48x48 dp. Aim for ~44-48px for main actions.
- Put space between adjacent tappable items.

### NO HOVER ON PHONES
Don't hide important actions behind `:hover`. Apply hover effects only where hover exists:
```css
@media (hover: hover) and (pointer: fine) {
  .row:hover .actions { opacity: 1; }
}
```

### FORMS THAT PHONES LOVE
```html
<input type="email" autocomplete="email" enterkeyhint="next">
<input type="tel" autocomplete="tel">
<input inputmode="decimal" autocomplete="off" placeholder="0.00">
<input autocomplete="one-time-code" inputmode="numeric">
```
- Right `type`/`inputmode` = the right keyboard
- `autocomplete` = autofill (huge time saver)
- Input font-size at least 16px, or iOS Safari zooms in on focus
- Labels above fields; show errors next to the field, in words

### THE THUMB ZONE
On big phones the top corners are hard to reach one-handed. Primary actions at the bottom; destructive actions away from frequent ones.

### MOTION AND COMFORT
Respect `@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce)`; support dark mode with `prefers-color-scheme` / `light-dark()`.

### ACCESSIBILITY IS NOW LAW IN THE EU
The European Accessibility Act applies since June 28, 2025 to many consumer digital products and services (e-commerce, banking, transport, e-books). WCAG 2.2 AA is the practical target. Basics: semantic HTML (`<button>`, not clickable `<div>`), labels, focus styles, contrast, alt text, screen-reader testing (VoiceOver, TalkBack).

### SOURCES
- https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/target-size-minimum.html
- https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility
- https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Reference/Global_attributes/inputmode
- https://commission.europa.eu/strategy-and-policy/policies/justice-and-fundamental-rights/disability/union-equality-strategy-rights-persons-disabilities-2021-2030/european-accessibility-act_en

nodes.title: Mobile performance & Core Web Vitals
nodes.content: ### THE THREE CORE WEB VITALS (measured at the 75th percentile of real users) | Metric | Measures | Good | |---|---|---| | LCP: Largest Contentful Paint | Loading: when the main content appears | <= 2.5 s | | INP: Interaction to Next Paint | Responsiveness: delay after taps/clicks, across the whole visit | <= 200 ms | | CLS: Cumulative Layout Shift | Visual stability: things jumping around | <= 0.1 | INP replaced FID in March 2024 and is the one most sites fail on phones: slow CPUs struggle with big JavaScript. ### WHY PHONES ARE THE HARD CASE The median mobile home page weighs ~2.2 MB (HTTP Archive Web Almanac 2025), and almost every page loads JavaScript. A mid-range phone parses and runs JS several times slower than your laptop. ### LCP FIXES - Serve AVIF/WebP images at the right size; never lazy-load the LCP image - `` or `` for the hero image - Fast server response (TTFB): caching, CDN - Fonts: `font-display: swap`, preload the main font, or use system fonts ### INP FIXES - Ship less JavaScript; split it and `defer` non-critical scripts - Break long tasks (>50 ms) into chunks: `await scheduler.yield()` (with a `setTimeout` fallback) - Keep event handlers short; do heavy work after the next paint or in a Web Worker - Avoid huge DOM trees (thousands of rows: paginate or virtualise) ### CLS FIXES - `width`/`height` or `aspect-ratio` on images, videos, iframes, ads - Reserve space for content that loads later - Animate `transform`/`opacity`, not `top`/`height` ### INSTANT NAVIGATIONS - Back/forward cache (bfcache): don't block it with `unload` handlers - Speculation Rules API (Chromium): prerender likely next pages for near-instant clicks ### MEASURE Lab: Lighthouse, PageSpeed Insights, DevTools Performance panel with CPU throttling. Field: Chrome UX Report (CrUX) data in PageSpeed Insights / Search Console, or the `web-vitals` JS library to collect your own. ### SOURCES - https://web.dev/articles/vitals - https://web.dev/articles/inp - https://almanac.httparchive.org/en/2025/page-weight - https://developer.chrome.com/docs/web-platform/prerender-pages

nodes.title: Start here: Baseline & Interop (what's safe to use)
nodes.content:
### BASELINE: ONE LABEL FOR "CAN I USE THIS?"
A feature is Baseline when it works in the current versions of Chrome, Edge, Firefox and Safari (desktop and mobile).
- Newly available: just reached all four engines; fine if your users update their browsers.
- Widely available: 30 months after that; safe almost everywhere.
- Each year gets a label ("Baseline 2026") listing what joined.
You'll see the Baseline badge on MDN pages, caniuse.com and webstatus.dev.

### BASELINE 2026 SO FAR (selected)
CSS: container style queries, `@scope`, `field-sizing`, `contrast-color()`, `shape()`, custom highlights, `:open`, active view transitions.
JS/APIs: Navigation API, Trusted Types, WebTransport, `Math.sumPrecise()`, `Iterator.concat()`, `Map.prototype.getOrInsert()`, modules in service workers, zstd compression.

### INTEROP 2026: WHAT BROWSERS ARE FIXING TOGETHER
Every year Apple, Google, Microsoft, Mozilla, Igalia and others pick focus areas to make consistent across browsers. Interop 2026 has 20, including: anchor positioning, advanced `attr()`, container style queries, `contrast-color()`, CSS `zoom`, dialog & popover additions, fetch upload streaming, the Navigation API, scoped custom element registries, scroll-driven animations, scroll snap, `shape()`, view transitions (incl. cross-document), WebRTC and WebTransport. These are the features most likely to become safe to use soon.

### HOW TO DECIDE IN PRACTICE
1. Check the feature's Baseline status on MDN.
2. Newly available: use it as progressive enhancement (works better where supported, still fine without).
3. Not Baseline: use `@supports` (CSS) or feature detection (`if ('popover' in HTMLElement.prototype)`) with a fallback.
4. Know your audience: an old kiosk tablet or locked-down corporate browser may be years behind.

### SOURCES
- https://web.dev/baseline/2026
- https://web.dev/blog/interop-2026
- https://webkit.org/blog/17818/announcing-interop-2026/
- https://webstatus.dev/

nodes.title: Modern CSS you can use now
nodes.content:
### LONG-AWAITED, NOW EVERYWHERE
- Nesting: `.card { & h2 { ... } &:hover { ... } }` (no Sass needed)
- `:has()`: the "parent selector": `form:has(input:invalid) button { opacity: .5; }`
- Container queries: components that adapt to their container
- Cascade layers: `@layer reset, base, components, utilities;` controls which styles win, regardless of specificity
- Subgrid: nested grids align with the parent's tracks
- Modern colour: `oklch()`, `color-mix(in oklch, var(--brand), white 20%)`, relative colours, `light-dark(#111, #eee)`
- Typography: `text-wrap: balance` for headings, `text-wrap: pretty` for paragraphs
- `@starting-style` + `transition-behavior: allow-discrete`: animate elements as they appear (and `display: none` transitions)
- `@property`: typed, animatable custom properties

### NEW IN BASELINE 2026
- `@scope (.card) to (.content) { ... }`: styles that apply only inside a component
- `field-sizing: content`: textareas and inputs that grow with their text
- `contrast-color(var(--bg))`: picks black or white text automatically
- `shape()`: responsive clip-path shapes with CSS units
- Anchor positioning (reached all engines in early 2026): tooltips and menus positioned relative to another element, no JS:
```css
.button { anchor-name: --menu-btn; }
.menu {
  position: absolute;
  position-anchor: --menu-btn;
  position-area: bottom span-right;
  position-try-fallbacks: flip-block; /* flips up if there's no room below */
}
```

### CHROMIUM-ONLY FOR NOW (use with @supports)
- `if()`: inline conditions, `width: if(media(width >= 40rem): 50%; else: 100%);`

- `appearance: base-select`: a fully stylable `<select>`

### A CAUTION
Old devices (like a smart TV or an old tablet stuck on an outdated browser) don't understand nesting or newer syntax: an unknown rule is simply ignored, which can break a layout silently. Know your target browsers.

JavaScript & TypeScript in 2026
nodes.content:
### TEMPORAL: DATES FINALLY FIXED
`Date` is mutable, timezone-confused and 0-indexed for months. Temporal (TC39 Stage 4) replaces it:
```js
const meeting = Temporal.ZonedDateTime.from('2026-10-14T09:30[Europe/Berlin]');
const later = meeting.add({ days: 7 });          // immutable: returns a new value
const today = Temporal.Now.plainDateISO();
const until = today.until('2026-12-25').days;    // days until Christmas
```
Shipped in Firefox 139, Chrome/Edge 144 (Jan 2026) and Node 26; Safari is the holdout (use `@js-temporal/polyfill`). Time to stop adding moment.js to new code.

### RECENT ADDITIONS WORTH KNOWING
- Iterator helpers: `map.values().filter(...).map(...).toArray()` (lazy, no intermediate arrays)
- Set methods: `a.union(b)`, `a.intersection(b)`, `a.difference(b)`, `a.isSubsetOf(b)`
- `Object.groupBy(items, item => item.category)`
- `Promise.withResolvers()`, `Promise.try()`, `Array.fromAsync()`
- `structuredClone(obj)`: deep copy
- `RegExp.escape(str)`, `Error.isError(x)`
- Uint8Array base64/hex: `bytes.toBase64()`, `Uint8Array.fromBase64(str)`
- Baseline 2026: `Math.sumPrecise([...])`, `Iterator.concat(a, b)`, `map.getOrInsert(key, default)`
- Navigation API (Baseline 2026): `navigation.addEventListener('navigate', e => e.intercept(...))`, a proper router primitive for SPAs

### TYPESCRIPT
- Used by the large majority of JS developers (State of JS 2025: ~40% write ONLY TypeScript).
- TypeScript 7 is the native (Go) rewrite of the compiler: roughly 10x faster type-checking.
- Node.js runs `.ts` files directly by stripping types (no build step for scripts).

### RUNTIMES
Node 24 is the active LTS; Node 26 is current. Deno 2 and Bun compete on speed and built-in tooling; all three run standard web APIs (`fetch`, Web Crypto, streams).

### NO-BUILD IS LEGITIMATE
Native ES modules + import maps + vendored library files (a `lib/` folder of downloaded library files) avoid npm and bundlers entirely. Fine for small apps; bundlers pay off for large apps, TypeScript, and heavy dependency trees.

nodes.title: Rendering patterns: MPA, SPA, SSR, islands, signals
nodes.content:
### WHERE IS THE HTML MADE?
| Pattern | How | Good for | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| MPA | Server renders every page | Content sites, forms, CRUD | Classic PHP, Laravel, Rails |
| SPA | Browser renders everything from JS | App-like tools behind a login | Vue/React apps (dashboards, admin panels) |
| SSR + hydration | Server renders HTML, then JS "hydrates" it to make it interactive | SEO + interactivity | Nuxt, Next.js, SvelteKit |
| SSG | HTML built once at deploy time | Docs, blogs, marketing | Astro, VitePress, Hugo |
| Islands | Mostly static HTML; only small interactive "islands" load JS | Content sites with some widgets | Astro, Fresh |
| Server Components | Components that run only on the server and send no JS | Big React apps | Next.js App Router |
| HTML over the wire | Server returns HTML fragments; a tiny library swaps them in | PHP/Rails devs who want interactivity without an SPA | htmx, Hotwire, Laravel Livewire |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    MPA["MPA: all server"] --- ISL["Islands / htmx: server + a little JS"] --- SSR["SSR + hydration: both"] --- SPA["SPA: all client"]
```

### SIGNALS: FINE-GRAINED REACTIVITY
A signal is a value that knows who depends on it, so only the exact DOM that uses it updates (no whole-component re-render). Vue's `ref()` has worked this way for years; Solid, Preact, Angular and Svelte 5 ("runes") adopted signals too. A TC39 proposal to standardise signals in JavaScript is in early stages.

### VUE IN 2026
Vue 3.6 (release candidate as of autumn 2026) brings Vapor Mode: opt-in, per-component compilation without a virtual DOM (Composition API / `<script setup>` only), plus a faster reactivity core based on "alien-signals".

### WHAT THE SURVEYS SAY
State of JS 2025: frameworks have stabilised; React remains most used, Vue and Svelte are well liked, and the action moved to meta-frameworks, with Astro scoring highest satisfaction.

### CHOOSING
Mostly content -> MPA/SSG/islands. Highly interactive tool behind a login -> SPA. Need both SEO and rich interactivity -> SSR framework. Coming from PHP and want "just a bit" of interactivity -> htmx or Alpine.js.

### SOURCES
- https://web.dev/articles/rendering-on-the-web
- https://docs.astro.build/en/concepts/islands/
- https://htmx.org/essays/
- https://github.com/tc39/proposal-signals

nodes.title: WebGPU, WebAssembly & AI in the browser
nodes.content:
### WEBGPU: THE GPU FROM JAVASCRIPT
The successor to WebGL, for both graphics and general GPU compute. Shipped in Chrome/Edge (2023), Safari 26 and Firefox (Windows first) in 2025, so it now reaches most users. It powers fast 3D (Three.js, Babylon.js) and running AI models in the browser.

### WEBASSEMBLY (WASM)
Run compiled C/C++/Rust/Go code in the browser at near-native speed: image/video editors (Figma, Photoshop web), SQLite in the browser, PDF tools, games. Wasm 3.0 (2025) added garbage collection (so Kotlin, Dart, Java compile to it well), 64-bit memory and exception handling. JSPI (letting Wasm call async web APIs) is an Interop 2026 focus area.

### AI MODELS RUNNING ON THE USER'S DEVICE
- Transformers.js / ONNX Runtime Web: run Hugging Face models (speech-to-text, translation, embeddings, image classification) in the browser with WebGPU or Wasm.
- WebLLM: chat-sized LLMs in the browser.
- Chrome's built-in AI APIs (Gemini Nano on device): Translator, Language Detector and Summarizer APIs shipped in Chrome; a Prompt API is available to extensions and in trials.
Why on-device: privacy (data never leaves the device), no per-request API cost, works offline. Why not: big model downloads, slower on weak phones, Chromium-only for the built-in APIs.

### OTHER NEW PLATFORM CAPABILITIES
- WebTransport (Baseline 2026): low-latency client-server messaging over HTTP/3 (successor to WebSockets for games/streaming)
- File System Access / Origin Private File System: fast local file storage
- Web Share, Web NFC, Web Bluetooth/USB (mostly Chromium): the "Project Fugu" APIs closing the gap with native apps

### SHOULD YOU CARE?
For CRUD apps: not much. But if you want offline AI features (summarise my notes, transcribe a voice memo) without sending data to the cloud, this is the toolbox.

### FOUR WAYS TO SHARE CODE ACROSS iOS AND ANDROID
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Q["One codebase, two platforms"] --> W["1. Web in a native shell"]
    Q --> J["2. JS/TS driving native UI"]
    Q --> R["3. Own rendering engine"]
    Q --> K["4. Shared logic, native or shared UI"]
    W --> W1["Capacitor (Ionic), PWAs, Tauri 2"]
    J --> J1["React Native + Expo, Lynx, Valdi, NativeScript"]
    R --> R1["Flutter (Dart), Compose Multiplatform"]
    K --> K1["Kotlin Multiplatform, .NET MAUI"]
```

### THE STATE OF PLAY
- React Native: the New Architecture is now the only architecture; Expo is the recommended way to start. Huge ecosystem, JS/TS skills transfer.
- Flutter: very popular, consistent pixel-perfect UI everywhere; finishing its move to the Impeller renderer; Dart.
- Kotlin Multiplatform + Compose Multiplatform: iOS support stable since May 2025; strongest with Android/Kotlin teams.
- Capacitor: your existing web app (Vue!) inside native apps with plugin access to device APIs; v8 shipped Dec 2025.
- PWAs: no store needed; much better on iOS than a few years ago, still with limits.

### NEW CHALLENGERS
- Lynx (ByteDance, open-sourced March 2025): web-like markup and real CSS, a Rust-powered dual-thread engine; powers parts of TikTok. Early ecosystem.
- Valdi (Snap, open-sourced Nov 2025): TypeScript compiled to native views, no web view, no JS bridge; used in Snapchat for 8 years but still labelled beta.
- Tauri 2: Rust + system WebView; mainly desktop, mobile is usable but less mature.

### TRENDS ACROSS ALL OF THEM
- Native-feeling performance is now expected: bridges are gone or minimised (RN's JSI, Lynx's threads).
- Over-the-air (OTA) JS updates without store review (Expo Updates, Capgo).
- AI tooling: MCP servers and agent workflows for building, running and testing on simulators.
- Platform deadlines drive work: edge-to-edge display on Android 15+, Swift Package Manager replacing CocoaPods on iOS.

nodes.title: React Native & Expo in 2026
nodes.content:
### WHAT IT IS
You write React components in JavaScript/TypeScript; React Native renders REAL native views (UIView, Android View). Same React skills as the web, native look and feel.

### THE NEW ARCHITECTURE IS THE ONLY ARCHITECTURE
- JSI: JavaScript calls native code directly (the old async JSON "bridge" is gone)
- Fabric: the new renderer (synchronous layout, concurrent React features)
- TurboModules: lazily loaded, typed native modules
Since RN 0.82 you can't turn it off; Expo SDK 55 dropped the legacy architecture entirely.

### RECENT RELEASES
- 0.84 (Feb 2026): Hermes V1 is the default JavaScript engine (faster startup, better performance)
- 0.86 (June 2026): full edge-to-edge support on Android 15+, DevTools improvements; the project moved to the new `react` GitHub organisation
- 0.87 (Aug 2026): strict TypeScript API by default, experimental Swift Package Manager support
- React 19.2 features and the React Compiler (automatic memoisation) are available

### EXPO: THE RECOMMENDED WAY TO START
The React Native docs recommend a framework, and Expo is it:
```bash
npx create-expo-app@latest my-app
npx expo start   # scan the QR code with the Expo Go app on your phone
```
- Expo Router: file-based navigation (like Nuxt/Next), native tabs
- EAS Build: builds iOS apps in the cloud (no Mac required to build)
- EAS Update: push JS fixes over the air, without a store review
- Config plugins and "prebuild": native projects generated for you, still customisable
- SDK releases track React Native (SDK 55 = RN 0.83, SDK 56 = RN 0.85, and onwards)

### STRENGTHS AND WEAKNESSES
+ React/TypeScript skills transfer; huge ecosystem; native UI; large job market
+ Web support via React Native Web / Expo for web
- Native modules sometimes needed for niche features (Swift/Kotlin)
- Upgrades used to be painful (much better with Expo)

nodes.title: Flutter in 2026
nodes.content:
### WHAT IT IS
Google's UI toolkit. You write Dart; Flutter draws every pixel itself with its own engine (it doesn't use native buttons). The result looks identical on iOS, Android, web and desktop.

### THE RENDERER: IMPELLER
Impeller replaced Skia to remove animation jank (it precompiles shaders). It's default on iOS and on Android API 29+; the 2026 roadmap removes the legacy Skia backend on Android 10+.

### FLUTTER & DART 2026 ROADMAP (official, "statement of intent")
- WebAssembly as the default for Flutter web builds
- Desktop multi-window support (with Canonical)
- Day-zero support for Android 17 and new iOS releases
- Material and Cupertino split out of the core into standalone packages
- GenUI SDK + A2UI protocol: interfaces generated by AI at runtime
- Exploring interpreted bytecode so parts of an app can update without a store release
- Dart language: primary constructors and augmentations
- AI developer tooling: MCP servers for Dart tooling, stateful hot reload in AI agents
- Full-stack Dart: Cloud Functions for Firebase, Genkit Dart

### A TASTE OF DART + FLUTTER
```dart
class Counter extends StatefulWidget {
  const Counter({super.key});
  @override
  State<Counter> createState() => _CounterState();
}

class _CounterState extends State<Counter> {
  int count = 0;
  @override
  Widget build(BuildContext context) => ElevatedButton(
        onPressed: () => setState(() => count++),
        child: Text('Tapped $count times'),
      );
}
```
Everything is a widget; hot reload updates the running app in under a second.

### STRENGTHS AND WEAKNESSES
+ Consistent UI and strong performance; excellent tooling and docs; one codebase for 6 platforms
+ Great for custom-branded designs and animation-heavy apps
- Doesn't use native controls (can feel "not quite iOS")
- Dart is another language to learn; web output is heavy and weak for SEO
- Larger app size than fully native

nodes.title: Capacitor: your web app in the app stores
nodes.content:
### WHAT IT IS
A native iOS/Android shell that runs YOUR web app (Vue, React, plain HTML) in a WebView, plus plugins that let JavaScript call native features: camera, files, push notifications, biometrics, haptics, share sheet, geolocation. Made by Ionic; the successor to Cordova; nearing a million downloads a week.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    VUE["Your Vue build (dist/)"] --> SHELL["Capacitor native shell"]
    SHELL --> WV["WebView runs the app"]
    WV <-->|"JS plugin calls"| NAT["Native APIs: camera, push, files, biometrics"]
    SHELL --> STORES["App Store + Play Store builds"]
```

### THE WORKFLOW
```bash
npm i @capacitor/core @capacitor/cli @capacitor/ios @capacitor/android
npx cap init
npx cap add ios && npx cap add android
npm run build          # build your web app as usual
npx cap sync           # copy it into the native projects
npx cap open ios       # opens Xcode (Android Studio for android)
```
```js
import { Camera, CameraResultType } from '@capacitor/camera';
const photo = await Camera.getPhoto({ resultType: CameraResultType.Uri });
```

### CAPACITOR 8 (December 2025) AND WHAT'S NEXT
- Swift Package Manager is the default for new iOS projects (CocoaPods still works for existing ones)
- Android edge-to-edge support through the new SystemBars plugin
- Capacitor 9 is forecast for late November 2026 (iOS 27 / Android 17 support)
- CocoaPods' trunk becomes read-only on December 2, 2026: migrate plugins and projects to SPM

### WHEN IT'S THE RIGHT CHOICE
+ You already have a good mobile-friendly web app and a web team
+ Business apps: forms, lists, dashboards, content
+ One codebase for web, iOS and Android, literally the same code
- Heavy animations, games, or very "native-feeling" gestures: choose React Native or Flutter
- You still need a Mac for iOS builds (or a cloud build service) and Apple/Google developer accounts

### TIP
Make the web app solid first (offline handling, touch targets, safe areas). Capacitor exposes every weakness of a desktop-first web app.

nodes.title: Kotlin & Compose Multiplatform
nodes.content:
### TWO LEVELS OF SHARING
- Kotlin Multiplatform (KMP): share business logic (networking, database, validation, models) in Kotlin; keep fully native UIs (SwiftUI on iOS, Jetpack Compose on Android). Adopt gradually, even one module at a time inside existing native apps.
- Compose Multiplatform (CMP): ALSO share the UI, written in Jetpack Compose, across Android, iOS, desktop and web.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph SHARED ["Shared Kotlin code"]
        LOGIC["Business logic, networking (Ktor), DB (SQLDelight / Room)"]
        UI["Optional: shared UI with Compose Multiplatform"]
    end
    LOGIC --> AND["Android app"]
    LOGIC --> IOS["iOS app (SwiftUI or Compose)"]
    UI --> AND
    UI --> IOS
```

### STATUS IN 2026
- KMP is stable and officially supported by Google for sharing logic with Android.
- Compose Multiplatform for iOS became stable with version 1.8.0 (May 2025); used in production apps (JetBrains cites Wrike, Markaz, Physics Wallah and others).
- Compose for web (Kotlin/Wasm) is in beta.
- Swift export and better Xcode integration keep improving iOS interop.

### STRENGTHS AND WEAKNESSES
+ Native performance; no JS runtime; real native APIs directly from Kotlin
+ Incremental adoption: no big rewrite; perfect for teams with Android/Kotlin experience
+ Android developers already know Compose
- iOS developers must accept Kotlin in their codebase
- Smaller ecosystem than React Native/Flutter; fewer tutorials
- Not a fit for web developers who don't know Kotlin

### THE CODE FEEL
```kotlin
@Composable
fun Greeting(name: String) {
    var clicks by remember { mutableStateOf(0) }
    Button(onClick = { clicks++ }) {
        Text("Hello $name, clicked $clicks times")
    }
}
```

nodes.title: PWAs in 2026
nodes.content:
### WHAT MAKES A WEB APP "PROGRESSIVE"
1. HTTPS
2. A web app manifest (name, icons, colours, `display: standalone`)
3. A service worker (offline caching, push notifications)
Then users can install it to their home screen; it opens in its own window like an app.
```json
{
  "name": "BudgetBee",
  "short_name": "BudgetBee",
  "start_url": "/budgetbee/",
  "display": "standalone",
  "background_color": "#111111",
  "theme_color": "#111111",
  "icons": [{ "src": "icon-512.png", "sizes": "512x512", "type": "image/png" }]
}
```

### A MINIMAL OFFLINE SERVICE WORKER
```js
// sw.js: network first, fall back to the cache when offline
self.addEventListener('fetch', (event) => {
  event.respondWith(
    fetch(event.request)
      .then((response) => {
        const copy = response.clone();
        caches.open('v1').then((cache) => cache.put(event.request, copy));
        return response;
      })
      .catch(() => caches.match(event.request))
  );
});
```
(Only cache GET requests in real code; register with `navigator.serviceWorker.register('sw.js')`.)

### THE iOS SITUATION
- Home-screen web apps support Web Push and app badges since iOS 16.4 (user must add to Home Screen first, then grant permission).
- Apple planned to drop home-screen web apps in the EU in early 2024, then reversed the decision; they still work there.
- Recent iOS versions open sites added to the Home Screen as web apps by default.
- Still limited: no install prompt in Safari (users use Share -> Add to Home Screen), weaker background capabilities, storage can be evicted if unused.

### ANDROID & DESKTOP
Chrome and Edge offer install prompts, push, background sync, file handling, share targets and many Project Fugu device APIs. You can even publish a PWA to Google Play (Trusted Web Activity) and the Microsoft Store using PWABuilder.

### WHEN A PWA IS ENOUGH
Internal tools, dashboards, content and utility apps, anything where app-store discovery doesn't matter. Upgrade to Capacitor when you need store presence or deeper native APIs.

nodes.title: How to choose a mobile approach
nodes.content:
### THE DECISION FLOW
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A{"Do you need the app stores or deep native features?"} -->|No| PWA["PWA"]
    A -->|Yes| B{"Do you already have a good web app and a web team?"}
    B -->|"Yes, and it's a business/content app"| CAP["Capacitor"]
    B -->|No, or performance/feel is critical| C{"Team background?"}
    C -->|"JavaScript / React"| RN["React Native + Expo"]
    C -->|"Kotlin / Android"| KMP["Kotlin + Compose Multiplatform"]
    C -->|"None yet / custom-designed UI"| FL["Flutter"]
```

### QUESTIONS TO ASK
1. Who builds and maintains it, and what languages do they know?
2. How "native" must it feel? (banking app vs internal checklist)
3. Performance needs: animations, lists of 10,000 items, camera processing?
4. Do you need the web version too, from the same code?
5. Offline requirements and device APIs (Bluetooth, NFC, background location)?
6. Hiring: React Native and Flutter have the largest job markets; KMP is growing.

### QUICK COMPARISON
| | Capacitor | React Native | Flutter | KMP/CMP |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Language | Your web stack | JS/TS + React | Dart | Kotlin |
| UI | Web (HTML/CSS) | Native views | Own renderer | Native or Compose |
| Reuse existing web app | Yes, fully | Logic only | No | No |
| Performance | Good for business apps | Very good | Very good | Native |
| Web target | Same code | React Native Web | Yes (Wasm) | Beta |

### A PATH FOR A VUE + PHP DEVELOPER
1. Make the web app mobile-first and installable (PWA).
2. Wrap it in Capacitor when you need the stores, push on iOS without "Add to Home Screen", or native APIs.
3. For career breadth, learn React Native with Expo: it's the most transferable "native" skill for a JavaScript developer.

nodes.title: Choosing a chart library
nodes.content:
### THE MAIN OPTIONS
| Library | Rendering | Strengths | Watch out |
|---|---|---|---|
| Chart.js | Canvas | Simplest API, most popular, responsive defaults; ships as one file you can vendor | Slows with very large datasets |
| Apache ECharts 6 | Canvas/SVG | Huge chart variety, dashboards, maps, big data, great on mobile | Large bundle; v6 changed module format |
| uPlot | Canvas | Tiny (~50 KB) and the fastest for big time-series | Fewer chart types; more manual styling |
| ApexCharts | SVG | Polished interactive defaults (zoom, annotations) | SVG slows with many points |
| D3 | SVG/Canvas | A toolkit, not a chart library: build anything | Steep learning curve; you write everything |
| Observable Plot | SVG | Concise D3-based "grammar of graphics" for exploration | Less interactive out of the box |
| Plotly.js | SVG/WebGL | Scientific charts, 3D, statistics | Heavy |
| Highcharts | SVG | Very complete, great accessibility | Commercial licence |
| Recharts / Nivo / visx | SVG | React-native APIs | React only |
Vue wrappers exist for most (vue-chartjs, vue-echarts).

### APACHE ECHARTS 6 (2025): WHAT'S NEW
New default theme with runtime theme switching and automatic dark mode, new chart types (chord, beeswarm, jittered scatter), broken axes for outliers, and a matrix coordinate system for laying out many small charts.

### HOW TO PICK
- A few standard charts in an admin page: Chart.js
- Dashboards, many chart types, large datasets, maps: ECharts
- Live metrics, 100k+ points: uPlot
- A unique custom visualisation: D3 (or Observable Plot first)
- Bundle size and "no build step": Chart.js, ECharts and uPlot all ship single-file browser builds you can vendor

### CHART.JS IN 10 LINES
```js
new Chart(document.getElementById('spend'), {
  type: 'line',
  data: {
    labels: ['Jan', 'Feb', 'Mar'],
    datasets: [{ label: 'Spending', data: [420, 380, 510], tension: 0.3 }],
  },
  options: { responsive: true, plugins: { legend: { display: false } } },
});
```

### DATAVIZ BASICS THAT MATTER MORE THAN THE LIBRARY
- Pick the chart for the question: trend = line, comparison = bar, part-of-whole = stacked bar (rarely pie)
- Start bar axes at zero; label units; avoid 3D and rainbow colours
- Colour-blind-safe palettes; don't rely on colour alone; provide the numbers as a table for screen readers

### SOURCES
- https://www.chartjs.org/docs/latest/
- https://echarts.apache.org/handbook/en/basics/release-note/v6-feature
- https://github.com/leeoniya/uPlot
- https://d3js.org/
- https://apexcharts.com/blog/state-of-javascript-charting-2026

nodes.title: Network graph libraries (nodes & edges)
nodes.content:
### WHEN YOU NEED ONE
Relationships rather than numbers: org charts, dependency graphs, knowledge graphs, social networks, workflow editors, mind maps, network topology.

### THE MAIN OPTIONS
| Library | Rendering | Best for |
|---|---|---|
| Cytoscape.js | Canvas | Graph analysis + visualisation: many layouts, graph algorithms (shortest path, centrality), good to a few thousand nodes |
| Sigma.js + graphology | WebGL | Large graphs (tens of thousands of nodes+); graphology provides the data model and algorithms |
| vis-network | Canvas | Quick interactive networks with physics; easy API (community-maintained) |
| AntV G6 | Canvas/WebGL | Feature-rich graph apps, many built-in behaviours and layouts |
| force-graph / 3d-force-graph | Canvas/WebGL (three.js) | Beautiful force-directed 2D/3D graphs with little code |
| React Flow / Vue Flow (xyflow) | DOM/SVG | Node-based EDITORS: workflow builders, pipelines, diagram tools users drag around |
| D3-force | SVG/Canvas | Full custom control |
| ELK.js / dagre | (layout only) | Clean layered layouts (flowcharts, dependency trees) to feed other renderers |
| Viz.js (Graphviz in Wasm) | SVG | Static, automatically laid-out diagrams from DOT text |

### PICKING
- Users EDIT the graph (drag nodes, connect ports): Vue Flow / React Flow
- Explore big data graphs: Sigma.js
- Analysis + moderate size + many layouts: Cytoscape.js
- A quick physics network for a demo: vis-network or force-graph
- Static diagrams in docs: Mermaid or Graphviz (next leaf)

### CYTOSCAPE.JS EXAMPLE
```js
cytoscape({
  container: document.getElementById('graph'),
  elements: [
    { data: { id: 'php' } }, { data: { id: 'mysql' } }, { data: { id: 'vue' } },
    { data: { source: 'vue', target: 'php' } },
    { data: { source: 'php', target: 'mysql' } },
  ],
  layout: { name: 'breadthfirst' },
  style: [{ selector: 'node', style: { label: 'data(id)' } }],
});
```

### PERFORMANCE RULES OF THUMB
SVG/DOM: up to ~1,000 elements. Canvas: thousands. WebGL: tens or hundreds of thousands. Beyond that, aggregate or filter before drawing: nobody can read 100,000 nodes anyway.

### SOURCES
- https://js.cytoscape.org/
- https://www.sigmajs.org/
- https://visjs.github.io/vis-network/docs/network/
- https://vueflow.dev/
- https://g6.antv.antgroup.com/en

nodes.title: Diagrams as code: Mermaid & friends
nodes.content:
### WHY TEXT DIAGRAMS
They live in git next to the code, show up in diffs and reviews, never need "the original Visio file", and AI assistants can write and update them. (Every diagram in Evolve is Mermaid text inside a leaf.)

### MERMAID (v11)
Renders in GitHub, GitLab, Obsidian, Notion and many docs tools. Diagram types: flowchart, sequence, class, state, ER, Gantt, pie, mindmap, timeline, quadrant, git graph, XY charts, Sankey, block, architecture and C4 (beta).
```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant A as PHP API
    participant D as MariaDB
    U->>A: PUT /api/notes/42
    A->>D: UPDATE notes SET body = ?
    D-->>A: OK
    A-->>U: {"ok": true}
```
The source of that diagram:
```
sequenceDiagram
    participant U as User
    participant A as PHP API
    U->>A: PUT /api/notes/42
    A-->>U: {"ok": true}
```

### THE ALTERNATIVES
| Tool | Strength |
|---|---|
| PlantUML | The most complete UML (Java-based) |
| Graphviz (DOT) | Excellent automatic layout of graphs |
| D2 | Modern syntax, pretty themes, good layouts |
| Structurizr DSL | C4 architecture models: one model, many views |
| Excalidraw | Hand-drawn whiteboard look; JSON files you can commit |
| draw.io (diagrams.net) | Free visual editor; stores XML, can embed in PNG/SVG |

### TIPS
- One idea per diagram; 5-15 boxes. Split instead of shrinking the font.
- Left-to-right (`flowchart LR`) for flows, top-down for hierarchies.
- Label the arrows: the verbs are the interesting part.
- Keep a legend if colours or shapes mean something.

### SOURCES
- https://mermaid.js.org/intro/
- https://d2lang.com/
- https://graphviz.org/
- https://excalidraw.com/

nodes.title: Start here: tests and docs are how teams scale
nodes.content:
### WHY THESE TWO BELONG TOGETHER
Both answer the same question for someone who isn't you (a teammate, future you, an AI agent): "How do I know this works, and how do I change it safely?"
- Tests: executable proof of what the code does
- Docs: the why, the how-to, and the big picture that code can't express

### THE AI-ERA TWIST
AI agents write more code than ever. Good tests let them check their own work; good docs (README, AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md, ADRs) give them the context to make the right change. Teams with both get far more out of AI tools.

### THIS SECTION
1. Testing: strategy, JS/Vue and PHP tools, end-to-end, APIs & mocking, test quality, what's new in 2026
2. Project documentation: what to write, READMEs, ADRs, diagrams, API docs, changelogs, docs for AI agents, keeping docs alive

See also "Testing strategy" in "Software Development using Claude" for TDD with an AI agent.

### SOURCES
- https://martinfowler.com/testing/
- https://diataxis.fr/

nodes.title: Start here: test types, shapes & test doubles
nodes.content:
### THE TEST TYPES
| Type | Checks | Speed |
|---|---|---|
| Static analysis | Types, lint rules (TypeScript, PHPStan, ESLint/Oxlint) | Instant |
| Unit | One function/class in isolation | ms |
| Component | One UI component rendered (Vue/React) | ms-s |
| Integration | Several parts together: API endpoint + real DB | s |
| Contract | Two services agree on an API's shape | s |
| End-to-end (E2E) | The whole app in a real browser, like a user | s-min |
| Visual regression | Screenshots didn't change unexpectedly | s |
| Non-functional | Performance, accessibility, security | varies |

### THE SHAPES (how much of each)
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph PYR ["Test pyramid"]
        P1["E2E: few"] --> P2["Integration: some"] --> P3["Unit: many"]
    end
    subgraph TRO ["Testing trophy"]
        T1["E2E: few"] --> T2["Integration: MOST"] --> T3["Unit: some"] --> T4["Static: base"]
    end
```
- Pyramid (classic): lots of fast unit tests.
- Trophy (Kent C. Dodds, popular for web apps): most value from integration tests that use the app like a user would, on top of static typing.
- Honeycomb (microservices): mostly integration/contract tests per service.
They agree on the real point: write tests that give confidence per minute spent, and keep E2E tests few but critical.

### TEST DOUBLES VOCABULARY
- Stub: returns canned answers ("getRate() returns 1.1")
- Mock: also verifies it was called a certain way
- Spy: records calls to a real function
- Fake: a working lightweight implementation (in-memory repository, fake mail server)
Mock at system boundaries (network, clock, payment provider), not your own internals: over-mocked tests pass while the real thing is broken.

### ARRANGE, ACT, ASSERT
Every test: set up the situation -> do the one thing -> check the outcome. One behaviour per test, named like a sentence: "rejects a transfer larger than the balance".

### SOURCES
- https://martinfowler.com/articles/practical-test-pyramid.html
- https://kentcdodds.com/blog/the-testing-trophy-and-testing-classifications
- https://martinfowler.com/bliki/TestDouble.html

nodes.title: Unit & component tests for JavaScript and Vue
PHP testing: PHPUnit & Pest
End-to-end testing with Playwright
nodes.content:
### WHY PLAYWRIGHT LEADS
State of JS 2025 named Playwright the "most adopted" testing tool. It drives real Chromium, Firefox and WebKit (Safari's engine), waits for elements automatically, runs tests in parallel, and its trace viewer shows a timeline of every action, screenshot and network call when a test fails.

### A TEST
```js
// tests/notes.spec.js
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test('user can create a note', async ({ page }) => {
  await page.goto('http://localhost:8080/');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'New note' }).click();
  await page.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Title' }).fill('My test note');
  await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' }).click();
  await expect(page.getByText('My test note')).toBeVisible();
});
```
`npx playwright test` runs it; `npx playwright test --ui` gives an interactive runner; `npx playwright codegen http://localhost:8080/` records your clicks as code.

### RULES FOR NON-FLAKY E2E TESTS
- Locate by role, label or `data-testid`; never by brittle CSS paths.
- Never `waitForTimeout(3000)`; use web-first assertions (`await expect(...).toBeVisible()`), which retry automatically.
- Each test creates its own data (via the API, faster than clicking) and doesn't depend on other tests.
- Log in once and reuse the saved storage state.
- Keep the suite small: critical journeys (sign up, log in, the main money-making flow), not every edge case.

### OTHER POWERS
- Network mocking: `page.route('**/api/**', ...)`
- API testing: the `request` fixture calls endpoints directly
- Visual comparisons: `await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot()`
- Mobile emulation: `devices['iPhone 15']`
- Accessibility checks with `@axe-core/playwright`

### CYPRESS
Still widely used (v15 in 2026, with AI "skills" for coding assistants). It runs inside the browser with a great interactive runner; Playwright wins on multi-browser support, parallelism and multi-tab/origin scenarios. For new projects most teams now choose Playwright.

### SOURCES
- https://playwright.dev/docs/intro
- https://playwright.dev/docs/best-practices
- https://playwright.dev/docs/trace-viewer
- https://2025.stateofjs.com/en-US/libraries/testing/

nodes.title: API tests, contract tests & mocking
Test quality: coverage, mutation testing, flakiness
nodes.content:
### COVERAGE: USEFUL, BUT NOT A GOAL
- Line coverage: which lines ran. Branch coverage: whether every `if` went both ways (more honest).
- Coverage tells you what is NOT tested; it can't tell you if tested code is tested WELL. A test with no assertions still produces coverage.
- 100% is rarely worth it; aim high on business rules, low on glue code. Tools: `vitest --coverage`, `phpunit --coverage-html` (needs Xdebug or PCOV).

### MUTATION TESTING: WHO TESTS THE TESTS?
The tool makes small changes ("mutants") to your code (`>` to `>=`, `+` to `-`, delete a line) and runs your tests. If the tests still pass, that mutant "survived": your tests don't really check that logic.
- JavaScript: Stryker. PHP: Infection. Java: PIT.
- Slow on big codebases: run on changed files or nightly.
- Especially valuable now that AI writes tests: it catches plausible-looking tests that assert nothing meaningful.

### FLAKY TESTS
A test that sometimes fails with no code change destroys trust: people start ignoring red builds.
Common causes: timing/race conditions, shared state between tests, test order dependence, real network calls, dates and time zones, random data, animations.
Fixes: deterministic clocks and seeds, isolated data per test, waiting on conditions instead of sleeping, mocking external services. Quarantine a flaky test (and fix it) rather than adding blind retries.

### OTHER GOOD HABITS
- Property-based testing (fast-check for JS, Eris for PHP): generate hundreds of random inputs and check a property ("sorting twice equals sorting once").
- Snapshot tests: fine for small, stable outputs; big snapshots get approved without reading.
- Test names that read as specifications; failure messages that say what was expected.
- Fast suites get run: keep unit tests in milliseconds, run the slow suite in CI.

### SOURCES
- https://stryker-mutator.io/
- https://infection.github.io/
- https://martinfowler.com/articles/nonDeterminism.html
- https://fast-check.dev/

nodes.title: What's new in testing (2025-2026)
nodes.content:
### FRAMEWORKS
- Vitest 4 (Oct 2025): browser mode is stable (separate provider packages like `@vitest/browser-playwright`), visual regression with `toMatchScreenshot()`, Playwright trace support.
- Jest 30 (2025): faster, lower memory, modern ESM/TypeScript handling; still the React Native default.
- Pest 4 (2025): browser testing, visual regression and smoke testing for PHP, on PHPUnit 12.
- Playwright: test agents, an MCP server and a token-efficient CLI for AI coding agents.
- Cypress 15: TypeScript 7 and Vite 8 support, AI "skills" for coding assistants.
- Survey trend (State of JS 2025): Vitest and Playwright are the most liked; Jest declining in new projects; `node:test` rising.

### AI IN TESTING
- Playwright test agents (since v1.56; `npx playwright init-agents`): a planner explores the app and writes a Markdown test plan, a generator turns it into tests, a healer repairs broken locators.
- Playwright MCP / CLI: lets Claude Code and other agents drive a real browser to check their own UI changes.
- AI-generated unit tests: fast to produce, but often "plausible tests that verify nothing" (empty assertions, mocks that drift from reality). Review them like any code, and use mutation testing to check they bite.
- Self-healing locators and autonomous QA agents in commercial tools; treat them as assistants, not replacements for deliberate test design.

### PRACTICES GAINING GROUND
- Visual regression as a normal part of component tests (no longer a separate paid service)
- Real-browser component testing instead of simulated DOMs
- Mutation testing to measure test quality
- Automated accessibility checks (axe-core) in E2E suites, driven by the EU Accessibility Act
- Testing LLM features with evals (see "Evals" in Core AI Concepts): you can't assert exact text, so you score outputs against criteria

### WHAT TO ACTUALLY DO
1. New JS project: Vitest + Testing Library + Playwright.
2. PHP: PHPUnit or Pest, plus PHPStan.
3. Let your AI agent run the tests (and Playwright) after every change; ask for failing tests first.

### SOURCES
- https://vitest.dev/blog/vitest-4
- https://playwright.dev/docs/test-agents
- https://pestphp.com/docs/pest-v4-is-here-now-with-browser-testing
- https://2025.stateofjs.com/en-US/libraries/testing/
- https://www.cypress.io/releases

nodes.title: Start here: what docs a project needs (Diátaxis)
nodes.content:
### THE FOUR KINDS OF DOCUMENTATION (Diátaxis)
| Type | Reader's goal | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Tutorial | Learn by doing (guided lesson) | "Build your first budget in BudgetBee" |
| How-to guide | Get a specific task done | "How to restore the database from a backup" |
| Reference | Look up facts | API endpoint list, config options, DB schema |
| Explanation | Understand why | "Why each service has its own database" |

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph STUDY ["When studying"]
        TUT["Tutorials: learning by doing"]
        EXP["Explanation: understanding"]
    end
    subgraph WORK ["When working"]
        HOW["How-to guides: tasks"]
        REF["Reference: facts"]
    end
```
The most common failure is mixing them: a reference page full of opinions, or a tutorial that stops to explain every design decision. Keep each page one type and link between them.

### THE MINIMUM SET FOR A REAL PROJECT
- README: what it is, how to run it (next leaf)
- CHANGELOG: what changed between versions
- LICENSE (and CONTRIBUTING / CODE_OF_CONDUCT if open source)
- `docs/adr/`: architecture decision records
- Architecture overview with a diagram
- API reference (OpenAPI) if others call your API
- Runbook: deploy, roll back, restore backups, rotate secrets, common incidents
- AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md for AI coding agents

### WRITE FOR A READER
Before writing, name the reader (new teammate? on-call engineer at 3 a.m.? API consumer?) and what they need to do next. Short sentences, examples first, copy-pasteable commands.

### SOURCES
- https://diataxis.fr/
- https://ubuntu.com/blog/diataxis-a-new-foundation-for-canonical-documentation
- https://www.writethedocs.org/guide/

nodes.title: Writing a great README
nodes.content:
### ITS JOB
In about 30 seconds a visitor should know: what is this, why should I care, and how do I run it?

### A TEMPLATE
````markdown
# BudgetBee

Personal budget tracker: income, expenses and savings goals.

![Screenshot](docs/screenshot.png)

## Features
- Import bank statements (CSV)
- Monthly spending by category

## Quick start
```bash
git clone https://github.com/you/budgetbee.git
mysql -u root -p < db/schema.sql
cp config.example.php config.php   # then fill in DB credentials
```
Open http://localhost:8080/

## Configuration
| Setting | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| DB_NAME | budgetbee | Database name |

## Development
- Run tests: `vendor/bin/phpunit`
- Project layout: `api/` PHP endpoints, `src/` Vue components

## Deployment / Contributing / License
...
````

### RULES
- Lead with a one-sentence description and a screenshot or GIF for anything visual.
- Commands must work when copy-pasted on a clean machine. Test them (or let CI test them).
- Show, don't tell: an example of usage beats a paragraph about it.
- Link out for depth (docs folder, ADRs) instead of a 3,000-line README.
- Status line if relevant: "Experimental", "Maintained", "Archived".
- Internal projects need READMEs too: "who owns this", "where it runs", "how to deploy".

### COMMON MISTAKES
Walls of text, missing setup steps ("install the usual stuff"), outdated commands, no mention of required environment variables, badges that hide the actual description.

### SOURCES
- https://www.makeareadme.com/
- https://github.com/RichardLitt/standard-readme
- https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/managing-your-repositorys-settings-and-features/customizing-your-repository/about-readmes

nodes.title: Architecture Decision Records (ADRs)
nodes.content:
### WHAT AN ADR IS
A short document recording ONE significant decision: the context, what you chose, and the consequences. Six months later, nobody remembers why you picked MariaDB over PostgreSQL or why sessions live in the DB. The ADR does.

### MICHAEL NYGARD'S ORIGINAL TEMPLATE
```markdown
# 3. One database per service

Date: 2026-03-02
Status: Accepted

## Context
Several small services share one database server. Mixing their tables in one
database makes backups, permissions and removing a service messy.

## Decision
Each service gets its own database, named after the service.

## Consequences
+ Services can be backed up, restored or deleted independently.
+ Clear ownership of tables.
- Cross-service queries need explicit cross-database joins.
- One more database to create for every new service.
```

### MADR 4 (a richer, maintained template)
Adds decision drivers, the options considered with pros/cons, and an optional YAML front matter for metadata (status, date, deciders). Good when decisions involve real trade-offs between alternatives.

### HOW TO RUN THEM
- Store in the repo: `docs/adr/0001-record-architecture-decisions.md`, `0002-...`. The first ADR records the decision to use ADRs.
- One decision per record, about a page long.
- Immutable once accepted: if you change your mind, write a NEW ADR that supersedes the old one, and mark the old one "Superseded by ADR-7".
- Write them for decisions that are hard to reverse or that people will question: databases, frameworks, auth approach, API style, hosting, data retention.
- Skip routine choices and implementation details.
- Review them in pull requests, like code.

### WHY THEY'RE EXTRA USEFUL NOW
They give AI agents and new teammates the "why" behind the code, so they don't "fix" deliberate decisions.

### SOURCES
- https://cognitect.com/blog/2011/11/15/documenting-architecture-decisions
- https://adr.github.io/madr/
- https://adr.github.io/

nodes.title: Architecture diagrams with the C4 model
nodes.content:
### THE PROBLEM WITH MOST ARCHITECTURE DIAGRAMS
Boxes and arrows with no legend, mixed abstraction levels (a server next to a class next to a team), and out of date. C4 (Simon Brown) fixes this with four zoom levels, like maps.

### THE FOUR LEVELS
1. System Context: your system as one box, plus its users and the external systems it talks to. For everyone, including non-technical people.
2. Container: the deployable/runnable parts: web app, API, database, queue, mobile app. ("Container" here means a runnable unit, not specifically Docker.)
3. Component: the main building blocks inside one container (controllers, services, repositories).
4. Code: classes. Usually skip it; your IDE can generate it, and hand-drawn ones go stale quickly.
Most teams only need levels 1 and 2.

### A CONTAINER DIAGRAM (level 2) FOR A SMALL WEB APP
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    U["Person: Household member"]
    subgraph SYS ["BudgetBee (software system)"]
        SPA["Container: Single-page app - Vue 3, in the browser"]
        API["Container: API - PHP 8.4 on Apache"]
        DB[("Container: Database - MariaDB")]
    end
    BANK["External system: Bank CSV exports"]
    U -->|"uses (HTTPS)"| SPA
    SPA -->|"JSON over HTTP"| API
    API -->|"reads/writes (PDO)"| DB
    U -->|"downloads statements from"| BANK
```

### NOTATION RULES THAT MAKE DIAGRAMS READABLE
- Every box: name, type, technology, one-line responsibility
- Every arrow: labelled with what flows and how (protocol)
- A title and a legend; one level per diagram
- Arrows point in the direction of the dependency/request

### TOOLING
- Mermaid: plain flowcharts as above, or its experimental `C4Context`/`C4Container` syntax
- Structurizr DSL: one model, many generated views (the C4 author's tool)
- PlantUML with the C4-PlantUML library
- IcePanel, draw.io for visual editing
Keep diagram source in the repo next to the docs so it changes with the code.

### SOURCES
- https://c4model.com/
- https://mermaid.js.org/syntax/c4.html
- https://structurizr.com/

nodes.title: API documentation with OpenAPI
nodes.content:
### OPENAPI IN ONE SENTENCE
A YAML/JSON description of your HTTP API (endpoints, parameters, request and response schemas, auth, errors) that both humans and tools can read.

### A MINIMAL SPEC
```yaml
openapi: 3.2.0
info:
  title: Notes API
  version: 1.0.0
paths:
  /api/notes:
    post:
      summary: Create a note
      requestBody:
        required: true
        content:
          application/json:
            schema:
              type: object
              required: [title]
              properties:
                title: { type: string, maxLength: 255 }
                body: { type: string }
                folderId: { type: [integer, 'null'] }
      responses:
        '201':
          description: The created note
        '400':
          description: Invalid input
          content:
            application/problem+json: {}
```

### WHAT 3.2 ADDED (September 2025, backward compatible with 3.1)
- Hierarchical tags (`parent`, `kind`, `summary`) for better navigation in big APIs
- The new HTTP `QUERY` method, plus `additionalOperations` for other methods
- First-class streaming responses (Server-Sent Events, JSON Lines) via `itemSchema`
- OAuth 2.0 Device Authorization flow, `oauth2MetadataUrl`, deprecating security schemes

### WHAT THE SPEC GIVES YOU
- Interactive docs: Swagger UI, Redoc, Scalar (try requests in the browser)
- Generated clients and server stubs (openapi-generator)
- Request/response validation in tests and at the gateway
- Linting for consistency (Spectral rulesets)
- Mock servers (Prism) before the backend exists
- AI agents and MCP tooling that understand your API

### DESIGN-FIRST VS CODE-FIRST
- Design-first: write the spec, review it with consumers, then implement. Best for public/partner APIs.
- Code-first: generate the spec from code annotations/attributes. Easier to keep in sync for internal APIs.

### GOOD API DOCS ALSO HAVE
A getting-started guide (auth + first request in 5 minutes), realistic examples for every endpoint, every error code explained, rate limits, versioning/deprecation policy and an API changelog. Event-driven APIs (webhooks, queues) can be described with AsyncAPI.

### SOURCES
- https://spec.openapis.org/oas/v3.2.0.html
- https://learn.openapis.org/
- https://redocly.com/blog/openapi-3-2
- https://stoplight.io/open-source/spectral

nodes.title: Changelogs, versioning & commit messages
nodes.content:
### SEMANTIC VERSIONING: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH
- PATCH (1.4.2 -> 1.4.3): bug fixes, nothing breaks
- MINOR (1.4.3 -> 1.5.0): new features, backwards compatible
- MAJOR (1.5.0 -> 2.0.0): breaking changes
`0.x` versions = anything may change. Alternative for apps: CalVer (`2026.10.1`), when "breaking" means little to users.

### KEEP A CHANGELOG
A human-written list of notable changes per version, newest first, with an "Unreleased" section at the top:
```markdown
# Changelog

## [Unreleased]
### Added
- Passkey login

## [1.5.0] - 2026-10-01
### Added
- Monthly spending chart
### Fixed
- Import failed on CSV files with a BOM
### Security
- Session cookie now uses SameSite=Lax
```
Groups: Added, Changed, Deprecated, Removed, Fixed, Security. Write for users, not as a dump of commit messages.

### CONVENTIONAL COMMITS
A commit message format that machines can read:
```
feat(import): support Excel bank statements
fix: keep leftover cents when splitting a bill
feat!: drop PHP 8.2 support

BREAKING CHANGE: requires PHP 8.3+
```
Types: `feat` (-> MINOR), `fix` (-> PATCH), `!` or `BREAKING CHANGE:` (-> MAJOR); also `docs`, `test`, `refactor`, `chore`, `perf`, `ci`.

### AUTOMATION
- release-please (Google): opens a release PR that bumps the version and updates CHANGELOG.md from conventional commits
- semantic-release, git-cliff, Changesets (popular in JS monorepos)
- commitlint in CI to enforce the format

### GOOD COMMIT MESSAGES (whatever the format)
- Imperative subject under ~72 chars: "Add passkey login", not "added stuff"
- Body explains WHY, and anything surprising

nodes.title: Docs for AI agents: AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, llms.txt
nodes.content:
### A NEW AUDIENCE FOR YOUR DOCS
AI coding agents read your repo before changing it. A short instruction file tells them what a new teammate would need on day one.

### AGENTS.MD: THE OPEN STANDARD
- A plain Markdown file at the repo root (and optionally in subfolders, where the nearest one wins).
- Introduced in 2025 by OpenAI with Google, Cursor, Sourcegraph, Factory and others; donated in December 2025 to the Linux Foundation's new Agentic AI Foundation (alongside Anthropic's MCP and Block's goose).
- Used by 60,000+ open-source projects and read by Codex, Cursor, GitHub Copilot, Gemini CLI, Devin, Amp and more.
- Tool-specific equivalents: CLAUDE.md (Claude Code), `.github/copilot-instructions.md`, Cursor rules. Many teams keep AGENTS.md as the source and point the others at it.

### WHAT TO PUT IN IT
```markdown
# AGENTS.md

## Commands
- Run tests: `vendor/bin/phpunit`
- Lint: `vendor/bin/phpstan analyse`

## Conventions
- PHP 8.4, PDO with prepared statements only
- Each service has its own database, named after the service
- Frontend: plain ES modules, no bundler; third-party files are vendored in /vendor

## Gotchas
- The dev server is already running on http://localhost:8080; don't start another one
- The warehouse scanners run an old Chrome: no CSS nesting in scanner pages
```
Keep it short and specific; rules the agent can act on, not an essay. Update it whenever an agent (or human) gets something wrong for lack of context.

### LLMS.TXT
A proposed convention (Jeremy Howard, 2024): a Markdown file at `/llms.txt` on your website listing your most useful docs pages for AI tools. Adoption grew fast through 2026, but server-log studies found most llms.txt files get almost no requests from AI crawlers, and major AI providers haven't committed to using it. Cheap to add for developer docs sites; don't expect miracles.

### DOCS AS TOOLS
MCP servers that serve up-to-date library docs to agents (e.g. Context7, vendor docs servers) reduce hallucinated APIs. Good, current reference docs now directly improve AI-written code.

### SOURCES
- https://agents.md/

- https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory
- https://llmstxt.org/

nodes.title: Docs-as-code & keeping docs alive
nodes.content:
### DOCS-AS-CODE
Treat documentation like source code:
- Plain text (Markdown) in the same repo as the code
- Changed in the same pull request as the code it describes
- Reviewed, versioned, and published automatically by CI
Result: docs stay in sync because updating them is part of "done".

### PUBLISHING TOOLS
VitePress (Vue-powered, fits Vue projects), Docusaurus (React), MkDocs Material (Python), Astro Starlight. All turn a `docs/` folder of Markdown into a searchable site.

### AUTOMATED CHECKS
- Broken links: lychee or markdown-link-check
- Prose style: Vale (enforce terms, flag passive voice or jargon)
- Code samples: run them in CI, or extract them from real tested files
- Spell checking: cspell

### HABITS THAT KEEP DOCS ALIVE
- "Docs updated?" as a pull-request checklist item
- Each doc has an owner and a "last reviewed" date
- Delete stale docs: wrong docs are worse than none
- Write the doc right after solving the problem (the runbook for that outage, the how-to for that tricky setup)
- Prefer generating reference docs (OpenAPI, DB schema, CLI help) over hand-writing them

### CODE COMMENTS ARE DOCUMENTATION TOO
- Explain WHY, not what: `// Retry once: the bank API returns 502 on its first call after idle`
- Docblocks for public functions (PHPDoc, JSDoc) help IDEs, static analysis and AI agents
- Delete commented-out code (git remembers it)

### RUNBOOKS & ONBOARDING
Two docs teams regret not having: a runbook ("the site is down: check X, then Y, restore with Z") and an onboarding guide ("your first day: get access, run the app, make a small change, deploy it").

- Generative AI: deep learning models that create text, images, audio, code
- Large language models (LLMs): generative models trained on text; the engine behind Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini

```mermaid
flowchart LR

```
