nodes.title: Types of learning
nodes.content:
### SUPERVISED LEARNING: LEARN FROM LABELLED EXAMPLES
You give inputs WITH the right answers; the model learns the mapping.
- Classification (pick a category): spam or not, which transaction category, is this X-ray abnormal
- Regression (predict a number): house price, delivery time, next month's spending

### UNSUPERVISED LEARNING: FIND STRUCTURE WITHOUT LABELS
- Clustering: group similar customers, transactions or documents
- Dimensionality reduction: squeeze 1,000 features into 2 for a chart
- Anomaly detection: flag the unusual card payment

### SELF-SUPERVISED LEARNING: THE DATA LABELS ITSELF
Hide part of the data and predict it. "The cat sat on the ___" -> "mat". No humans needed to label, so you can train on trillions of words. This is how LLMs are pre-trained.

### REINFORCEMENT LEARNING (RL): LEARN BY TRIAL, ERROR AND REWARD
An agent acts, gets a reward or penalty, and improves its strategy (policy). Classic: game-playing (AlphaGo). Modern: training LLMs to reason by rewarding correct answers on maths and code problems that can be checked automatically.

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    D{"What data do you have?"} -->|"inputs + correct answers"| S["Supervised"]
    D -->|"just inputs"| U["Unsupervised"]
    D -->|"raw data where parts can be hidden and predicted"| SS["Self-supervised"]
    D -->|"an environment that gives rewards"| RL["Reinforcement learning"]
```

### DO YOU EVEN NEED ML?
If you can write the rule ("amount > 1000 and new payee -> review"), write the rule. ML pays off when the rules are too many, too fuzzy or keep changing. And in 2026, many classic ML tasks (classifying text, extracting fields) are simply done by prompting an LLM, with no training at all.

### SOURCES
- https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/intro-to-ml
- https://www.coursera.org/specializations/machine-learning-introduction
- https://scikit-learn.org/stable/tutorial/basic/tutorial.html

nodes.title: How models learn: loss, gradient descent, overfitting
nodes.content:
### THE TRAINING LOOP
A model is a function with adjustable numbers (parameters / weights). Training finds the weights that make its predictions match the data.
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    X["Training example"] --> M["Model makes a prediction"]
    M --> L["Loss: how wrong was it?"]
    L --> G["Gradient: which way should each weight move?"]
    G --> U["Nudge all weights a little"]
    U --> M
```
- Loss function: a single number for "how wrong" (e.g. mean squared error for numbers, cross-entropy for categories and next-token prediction).
- Gradient descent: compute the slope of the loss for every weight and step "downhill". The learning rate is the step size: too big and it overshoots, too small and it takes forever.
- Batch: a handful of examples per step. Epoch: one pass over the whole dataset.

### SPLIT YOUR DATA THREE WAYS
- Training set (~70-80%): the model learns from it
- Validation set (~10-15%): you tune settings (model size, learning rate) against it
- Test set (~10-15%): touched ONCE at the end, for an honest score
Using test data during development is "data leakage": your score will be too good to be true.

### OVERFITTING VS UNDERFITTING
- Overfitting: memorises the training data, including its noise; great on training data, poor on new data. Like a student who memorised last year's exam answers.
- Underfitting: too simple to capture the pattern; poor everywhere.
- Remedies for overfitting: more data, simpler model, regularisation, dropout, early stopping (stop when validation loss starts rising).

### MEASURE THE RIGHT THING (spam filter example)
- Accuracy can lie: if 1% of email is spam, "never spam" is 99% accurate and useless.
- Precision: of the emails flagged as spam, how many really were? (false alarms)
- Recall: of all the real spam, how much did we catch? (misses)
- F1: the balance of the two. Choose based on which mistake costs more.

### THE UNGLAMOROUS TRUTH
Data quality beats clever algorithms: clean labels, representative examples, no leakage. Most ML project time is data work.

### SOURCES
- https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/crash-course
- https://www.3blue1brown.com/lessons/gradient-descent
- https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/crash-course/classification/accuracy-precision-recall

nodes.title: Neural networks & deep learning
nodes.content:
### A NEURON
Takes some numbers, multiplies each by a weight, adds them up plus a bias, and passes the result through an activation function (e.g. ReLU: "negative becomes 0"). Alone it's trivial. Millions or billions of them, in layers, can approximate almost any function.

### LAYERS
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    I1(("input")) --> H1(("hidden")) --> O(("output"))
    I1 --> H2(("hidden"))
    I2(("input")) --> H1
    I2 --> H2
    H2 --> O
```
- Input layer: the raw numbers (pixels, token embeddings)
- Hidden layers: each learns more abstract features (edges -> shapes -> faces)
- Output layer: the prediction (class probabilities, the next token)
"Deep" learning = many hidden layers.

### BACKPROPAGATION
The algorithm that computes the gradient for every weight efficiently, by passing the error backwards from the output through the layers (the chain rule from calculus). It's what makes gradient descent possible on huge networks.

### FAMOUS ARCHITECTURES
| Architecture | Idea | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| CNN (convolutional) | Small filters slide over an image | Image recognition (still common) |
| RNN / LSTM | Process a sequence one step at a time with memory | Older speech/text models; largely replaced |
| Transformer | Attention: every element looks at every other at once | LLMs, and increasingly vision, audio, everything |
| Diffusion model | Learn to remove noise step by step | Image and video generation |
| Mixture of Experts (MoE) | Many sub-networks; each token only uses a few | Large modern LLMs (cheaper per token) |

### WHY GPUs
Neural networks are mostly giant matrix multiplications; GPUs (and TPUs, Trainium) do thousands of them in parallel. That, plus huge datasets, is why deep learning took off after 2012.

### EMBEDDINGS: A KEY IDEA
Networks turn things (words, images, users) into lists of numbers where similar things end up close together. These learned representations power search, recommendations and RAG (see "Embeddings & vector search").

### SOURCES
- https://www.3blue1brown.com/topics/neural-networks
- https://www.deeplearning.ai/courses/deep-learning-specialization/
- https://playground.tensorflow.org/ (play with a tiny network in your browser)

nodes.title: Transformers & attention
nodes.content:
### THE PIPELINE
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    T["Text"] --> TK["Tokenizer: text -> token IDs"]
    TK --> E["Embeddings: each token -> a vector"]
    E --> L["Transformer layers x N (attention + feed-forward)"]
    L --> P["Probabilities for every possible next token"]
    P --> S["Pick one token"]
    S -->|"append and repeat"| TK
```
An LLM does exactly one thing: given the tokens so far, predict a probability for each possible next token. Everything else (answers, code, reasoning) comes from repeating that very well.

### ATTENTION IN PLAIN WORDS
In "The animal didn't cross the street because IT was too tired", what does "it" refer to? Attention lets each token look at every other token and decide which ones matter for its meaning.
- Each token produces a Query ("what am I looking for?"), a Key ("what do I contain?") and a Value ("what I'll pass on").
- A token's query is compared with every key; high matches get more weight; it takes a weighted mix of their values.
- Multi-head attention: many attention "heads" in parallel, each tracking a different kind of relationship (grammar, references, topic).

### THE REST OF A LAYER
After attention, a feed-forward network processes each token's vector; most of the model's "knowledge" is thought to be stored in these weights. Stack dozens of such layers and you get a modern LLM with billions of parameters.

### WHY IT WON
Older sequence models (RNNs) read one word at a time. Transformers process all tokens in parallel, which suits GPUs and scales to enormous training runs.

### WHY LONG CONTEXT COSTS MORE
Attention compares every token with every other: cost grows roughly with the square of the length. Tricks like the KV cache (reuse computed keys/values while generating), efficient attention variants and prompt caching keep it practical, but a 500k-token prompt is still slower and pricier than a 5k one, and models can lose track of details in very long contexts.

### SOURCES
- https://www.3blue1brown.com/lessons/attention
- https://jalammar.github.io/illustrated-transformer/
- https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762
- https://poloclub.github.io/transformer-explainer/ (interactive)

nodes.title: Training an LLM: pre-training to post-training
nodes.content:
### STAGE 1: PRE-TRAINING (the expensive part)
Next-token prediction on trillions of tokens of text and code (web, books, papers, code repositories). Self-supervised: the text is its own answer key. Takes thousands of GPUs for weeks to months. The result is a "base model": very knowledgeable, but it just continues text; ask it a question and it may reply with more questions.
Knowledge cutoff: the model only knows what was in its training data up to that date.

### STAGE 2: SUPERVISED FINE-TUNING (SFT)
Train on many examples of good conversations (instruction -> ideal response) so it behaves like an assistant: answers questions, follows formats, uses tools.

### STAGE 3: PREFERENCE TUNING
Teach it which of two answers is better: more helpful, more honest, safer.
- RLHF: humans rank answers, a reward model learns their preferences, RL optimises the LLM against it.
- DPO: a simpler method that learns directly from preference pairs.
- Constitutional AI / RLAIF (Anthropic): the model critiques and revises answers against written principles, with AI feedback replacing much of the human labelling.

### STAGE 4: REINFORCEMENT LEARNING FOR REASONING
Give the model problems with checkable answers (maths, code with tests, puzzles) and reward correct final results. Models learn to think step by step, try approaches, notice mistakes and backtrack. This is what created "reasoning models" and is the main driver of recent progress, especially for coding agents.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    PT["Pre-training: knowledge"] --> SFT["SFT: assistant behaviour"] --> PREF["Preference tuning: helpful, harmless, honest"] --> RL["RL on verifiable tasks: reasoning, agentic skills"]
```

### OTHER TERMS YOU'LL HEAR
- Scaling laws: loss improves predictably with more parameters, data and compute.
- Distillation: a small model trained to imitate a big one (cheap, fast models).
- Synthetic data: training examples generated by other models.
- Open-weight vs closed: open-weight models publish their weights (Llama, Qwen, Mistral, DeepSeek, Gemma, gpt-oss); closed ones are API-only (Claude, GPT, Gemini).

### SOURCES
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155 (InstructGPT: SFT + RLHF)
- https://www.anthropic.com/research/constitutional-ai-harmlessness-from-ai-feedback
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948 (DeepSeek-R1: RL for reasoning)
- https://huggingface.co/learn/llm-course

nodes.title: Generation: sampling, temperature & cost
nodes.content:
### HOW A RESPONSE IS PRODUCED
The model outputs a probability for every token in its vocabulary (often 100k+). One is picked, appended, and the whole thing repeats until a stop token or the token limit. That's why responses stream in word by word.

### SAMPLING SETTINGS
- Temperature: 0 = almost always the most likely token (focused, repetitive); ~1 = more varied, creative. Low for extraction and code, higher for brainstorming.
- Top-p (nucleus): only sample from the smallest set of tokens whose probabilities add up to p (e.g. 0.9). Top-k: only the k most likely.
- Max tokens: a hard cap on output length (a response cut off mid-sentence usually hit this).
- Stop sequences: strings that end generation.
Even at temperature 0, outputs aren't guaranteed identical across calls (batching and hardware effects). Design for variation.

### WHY LLMs STRUGGLE WITH CERTAIN THINGS
- Counting letters or reversing words: they see tokens (word pieces), not characters.
- Exact arithmetic on long numbers: better done with a tool (code execution).
- Facts after the knowledge cutoff: they need search or retrieval.

### CONTEXT WINDOW = WORKING MEMORY
Everything the model "knows" during a request: system prompt + conversation + documents + tool results + the output being written. Nothing persists between API calls unless you send it again (or use a memory tool). See "Tokens & the context window" in the Claude section for numbers and limits.

### SPEED AND COST
- Time to first token (latency) and tokens per second (throughput) are separate metrics.
- Output tokens cost several times more than input tokens.
- Reasoning ("thinking") tokens are output tokens: hard problems cost more.
- Prompt caching makes repeated long prefixes (system prompts, documents) much cheaper and faster.
- Batch APIs trade speed for ~50% discounts on non-urgent work.

### THE MENTAL MODEL
An LLM is not a database lookup. It's a very well-trained predictor that reconstructs plausible text. Great at language, patterns, code and reasoning; it needs grounding (documents, tools, tests) for facts and exactness.

### SOURCES
- https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/models/overview
- https://huggingface.co/blog/how-to-generate
- https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching

nodes.title: Reasoning models & test-time compute
nodes.content:
### THE IDEA
Instead of answering immediately, the model first generates a long internal chain of thought: plans, tries approaches, checks its work, backtracks. More thinking at answer time ("test-time compute") buys better answers on hard problems.

### HOW WE GOT HERE
- 2022: "chain-of-thought" prompting ("think step by step") showed that writing out reasoning improves accuracy.
- Sept 2024: OpenAI o1, the first model trained with RL specifically to reason before answering.
- Jan 2025: DeepSeek-R1 published an open-weight reasoning model and its RL recipe.
- 2025-2026: every frontier lab ships reasoning: Claude's extended/adaptive thinking with an effort setting, Gemini's thinking modes, GPT-5's reasoning levels; open models (Qwen, DeepSeek, gpt-oss) too.

### TRAINING SCALING VS TEST-TIME SCALING
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Old lever: bigger model + more training data"] --> Q["Better answers"]
    B["New lever: more thinking tokens per question"] --> Q
```
The new lever is flexible: spend little on easy questions, a lot on hard ones.

### WHEN TO USE REASONING
- Worth it: multi-step maths, tricky debugging, architecture decisions, planning, agentic coding, analysing long documents
- Not worth it: simple lookups, formatting, classification, chit-chat (slower and pricier for no gain)
Most APIs let you set a thinking budget or effort level; start low and raise it only when quality needs it.

### CAVEATS
- Thinking costs output tokens and adds latency (seconds to minutes).
- The visible reasoning summary isn't a guaranteed faithful record of how the model reached its answer: verify results, not the narrative.
- More thinking doesn't fix missing knowledge: give it the documents or tools.
- Reasoning models can "overthink" simple tasks; give clear, direct instructions.

### WHY IT MATTERS FOR DEVELOPERS
Reasoning + tool use is what makes coding agents work: read the code, form a hypothesis, run the tests, adjust. See "Thinking & effort" in the Claude section for the API side.

### SOURCES
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11903 (chain-of-thought prompting)
- https://openai.com/index/learning-to-reason-with-llms/
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948
- https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/extended-thinking

nodes.title: Multimodal & generative media
nodes.content:
### BEYOND TEXT
Modern frontier models are multimodal: they take images, PDFs, screenshots and sometimes audio/video as input, and some generate images or speech.

### VISION-LANGUAGE MODELS
Images are cut into patches and turned into tokens the transformer reads alongside text. Practical uses for developers:
- "Here's a screenshot of the bug": UI debugging
- Read charts, scanned receipts, handwritten notes, invoices
- Compare a design mock-up with the implemented page
- Computer use: models operating apps by looking at the screen and clicking

### SPEECH
- Speech-to-text (ASR): Whisper-style models, now very accurate and runnable locally
- Text-to-speech: natural voices
- Speech-to-speech "realtime" models: voice conversations without separate transcription (low latency)

### IMAGE GENERATION: DIFFUSION
Training: take real images, add noise step by step, and teach a network to predict and remove the noise. Generation: start from pure noise and denoise it, step by step, guided by your text prompt (via a text encoder). Examples: Stable Diffusion, Flux, Midjourney, Imagen. Some newer models (e.g. GPT-image) generate images autoregressively, token by token, and follow instructions and text in images better.

### VIDEO AND AUDIO GENERATION
2025 was a jump year: Google's Veo 3 and OpenAI's Sora 2 generate video with synchronised sound. Music generation (Suno, Udio) went mainstream too, along with lawsuits about training data.

### MULTIMODAL EMBEDDINGS
Models like CLIP put images and text into the same vector space, so "red bicycle" finds photos of red bicycles: the basis of image search.

### THINGS TO WATCH
- Cost: images and audio consume many tokens
- Hallucinated details in images (wrong numbers read from a blurry chart)
- Provenance: C2PA "content credentials" and watermarking (e.g. Google's SynthID) to label AI-generated media; the EU AI Act requires labelling of deepfakes
- Copyright and consent, especially for voices and faces

### SOURCES
- https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/vision
- https://huggingface.co/learn/diffusion-course
- https://c2pa.org/
- https://deepmind.google/models/veo/

nodes.title: Embeddings & vector search
nodes.content:
### WHAT AN EMBEDDING IS
A list of numbers (a vector, often 768-3,072 dimensions) that represents the MEANING of a piece of text (or an image). Texts with similar meaning get vectors that point in similar directions, even with no words in common: "cheap flights" is close to "budget airline tickets".

### MEASURING CLOSENESS
Cosine similarity: 1 = same direction (same meaning), 0 = unrelated. Most vector search uses cosine distance (1 - similarity) or dot product.

### THE WORKFLOW
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    DOCS["Your documents"] --> EM["Embedding model"] --> VDB[("Vector index")]
    Q["Search query"] --> EM2["Same embedding model"] --> NN["Find nearest vectors"]
    VDB --> NN --> R["Most similar documents"]
```
Always embed documents and queries with the SAME model.

### EMBEDDING MODELS
API: Voyage AI (recommended in Anthropic's docs), OpenAI text-embedding-3, Cohere, Google Gemini embeddings. Open/local: EmbeddingGemma, BGE, nomic-embed, Qwen3-Embedding (run them with Ollama or Transformers.js). Check the MTEB leaderboard for your language and task.

### VECTOR SEARCH IN MARIADB 11.8 (handy if you already run MariaDB)
```sql
CREATE TABLE note_vectors (
  note_id INT UNSIGNED PRIMARY KEY,
  embedding VECTOR(768) NOT NULL,
  VECTOR INDEX (embedding) DISTANCE=cosine
);

-- the 5 notes closest in meaning to a query vector
SELECT note_id
FROM note_vectors
ORDER BY VEC_DISTANCE_COSINE(embedding, VEC_FromText(?))
LIMIT 5;
```
Pass the query's embedding as a JSON-style array string, e.g. `'[0.12, -0.03, ...]'`.

### OTHER VECTOR STORES
pgvector (PostgreSQL), Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus, Chroma, Pinecone, Amazon S3 Vectors, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch. For under a million vectors, the database you already run is usually enough.

### EXACT VS APPROXIMATE SEARCH
Comparing against every vector is exact but slow at scale. Indexes like HNSW (a navigable graph of vectors) find "nearly the best" matches in milliseconds: a small loss of recall for a huge speed-up.

### USES
Semantic search, RAG retrieval, "related notes", duplicate detection, clustering topics, recommendations, classification by nearest examples.

### SOURCES
- https://mariadb.com/kb/en/vectors/
- https://github.com/pgvector/pgvector
- https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/embeddings
- https://huggingface.co/spaces/mteb/leaderboard

nodes.title: RAG: retrieval-augmented generation
nodes.content:
### THE PROBLEM IT SOLVES
LLMs don't know your private documents or anything after their cutoff, and they may make things up. RAG retrieves relevant passages first and puts them in the prompt: "Answer using only these sources, and cite them."

### THE PIPELINE
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph INGEST ["Ingest (once, and on every change)"]
        D["Documents"] --> C["Split into chunks"] --> E["Embed + keyword index"] --> S[("Search index")]
    end
    subgraph ANSWER ["Answer (every question)"]
        Q["Question"] --> H["Hybrid search: vectors + keywords"] --> RR["Rerank top ~50"] --> P["Top 5-10 chunks into the prompt"] --> L["LLM answers with citations"]
    end
    S --> H
```

### 2026 BEST PRACTICE
- Hybrid search: run keyword search (BM25, great for names, codes, exact terms) AND vector search (great for meaning), then merge the lists with Reciprocal Rank Fusion.
- Rerank: a cross-encoder reranker re-scores the top ~50-100 candidates against the question: usually the biggest single quality gain.
- Chunking: ~256-512 tokens, split on structure (headings, paragraphs, functions), small overlap, keep metadata (title, date, source URL).
- Contextual retrieval (Anthropic, 2024): before embedding, prepend a sentence of context to each chunk ("This chunk is from the 2025 refund policy, section on digital goods"). Anthropic reported 49% fewer failed retrievals, 67% combined with reranking.
- Agentic RAG: give the model a search TOOL and let it search, read, and search again for multi-step questions.

### WHEN YOU DON'T NEED RAG
If all your material fits comfortably in the context window (say, under a few hundred pages) just include it, with prompt caching to keep it cheap. RAG is for large or fast-changing collections.

### HOW RAG FAILS (and what to check)
1. The right chunk was never retrieved (measure retrieval recall on test questions)
2. It was retrieved but ignored or misread (faithfulness)
3. The source itself is outdated or contradictory
Build a small test set of real questions with known answers and track: retrieval hit rate, answer correctness, citation accuracy.

### SECURITY NOTE
Retrieved documents are untrusted input: a document can contain injected instructions. Treat them as data, and respect user permissions in retrieval (don't retrieve documents the user can't see).

### SOURCES
- https://www.anthropic.com/news/contextual-retrieval
- https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/embeddings
- https://www.pinecone.io/learn/retrieval-augmented-generation/
- https://docs.ragas.io/

nodes.title: Prompting vs RAG vs fine-tuning
nodes.content:
### THE LADDER (climb only as high as you need)
1. Better prompting: clear instructions, examples (few-shot), structure, the right model. Solves most problems.
2. RAG / tools: when the model lacks KNOWLEDGE (your docs, live data).
3. Fine-tuning: when you need a consistent BEHAVIOUR, style or format that prompting can't reliably get, or a smaller/cheaper model to do one narrow task well.
4. Distillation: train a small model on a big model's outputs for cheap, fast, high-volume tasks.

| Need | Best tool |
|---|---|
| Answer questions about our wiki | RAG |
| Always reply in our JSON schema | Structured outputs (no training needed) |
| Match our brand voice exactly | Prompting with examples; fine-tune if that fails |
| Classify 10M support tickets cheaply | Fine-tuned or distilled small model |
| Know events after the cutoff | Search / RAG |
| Learn a new skill end to end | Usually not achievable by your own fine-tuning |

### FINE-TUNING FACTS
- It's better at teaching FORM (style, format, tone, task focus) than FACTS. Facts added by fine-tuning are unreliable and go stale; use retrieval for facts.
- LoRA / QLoRA: train small "adapter" matrices on top of a frozen base model: tens of dollars of GPU time instead of a cluster; you can swap adapters per task.
- Data: hundreds to a few thousand high-quality examples for style/format; quality beats quantity. If you have fewer than a few hundred, few-shot prompting usually wins.
- Costs beyond training: evaluation, hosting, and redoing it when a better base model comes out (which happens every few months).

### THE PRACTICAL ORDER
Prompt -> evaluate -> add retrieval/tools -> evaluate -> fine-tune only if a measured gap remains. You can't decide if fine-tuning helped without an eval set (see "Evals" in the Claude section).

### SOURCES
- https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-engineering/overview
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685 (LoRA)
- https://huggingface.co/docs/peft/index
- https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/model-optimization

nodes.title: Agents, tools & protocols (MCP, A2A, Skills)
nodes.content:
### WHAT MAKES SOMETHING AN AGENT
An LLM that runs in a LOOP, deciding which tools to call, seeing the results, and continuing until the task is done.
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    G["Goal"] --> T["Think: what next?"]
    T --> A["Act: call a tool (search, read file, run tests, query DB)"]
    A --> O["Observe the result"]
    O --> T
    T -->|"done"| R["Final answer / finished change"]
```
Ingredients: a capable model, well-designed tools, a way to remember (context, notes, memory files), and guardrails (permissions, human approval for risky actions).

### WORKFLOWS VS AGENTS (Anthropic's "Building effective agents")
- Workflows: YOU define the steps in code (prompt chaining, routing, parallel calls, orchestrator-workers, evaluator-optimizer loops). Predictable, cheaper, easier to test.
- Agents: the MODEL decides the steps. Flexible, for open-ended tasks (coding, research).
Start with the simplest thing (often a single well-prompted call), add workflow steps, and reach for a full agent only when the path truly can't be predicted.

### THE PROTOCOLS
- MCP (Model Context Protocol, Anthropic 2024): a standard way to plug tools and data sources into any AI app: one MCP server for your database works with Claude, ChatGPT, Cursor, VS Code... Donated to the Linux Foundation's Agentic AI Foundation in Dec 2025. A mid-2026 spec revision made servers stateless, so they scale behind normal load balancers.
- A2A (Agent2Agent, Google 2025, now also at the Linux Foundation): how agents from different vendors discover each other and delegate tasks.
- Agent Skills (Anthropic, published as an open standard in late 2025): folders of instructions + scripts an agent loads only when relevant, a way to package know-how without bloating context.
- AGENTS.md: project instructions for coding agents (see Engineering Practices).

### MULTI-AGENT SYSTEMS
An orchestrator splits work across sub-agents with their own clean contexts (research in parallel, review each other's work). Powerful for broad tasks, but costs multiply and errors can compound.

### THE RISKS
More autonomy = more damage when wrong: excessive agency, prompt injection through tool results, runaway costs. Least-privilege tools, sandboxes, budgets, and human confirmation for destructive or outward-facing actions.
For building agents with the Claude API and Agent SDK, see "Agents: which way to build one" and "MCP: exposing your app to AI" in the Claude section.

### SOURCES
- https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/building-effective-agents
- https://modelcontextprotocol.io/
- https://a2a-protocol.org/
- https://agentskills.io/

nodes.title: Context engineering
nodes.content:
### FROM PROMPT ENGINEERING TO CONTEXT ENGINEERING
Prompt engineering = writing good instructions. Context engineering (Anthropic's term, 2025) = curating EVERYTHING the model sees at each step: system prompt, tool definitions, examples, conversation history, retrieved documents, tool results, memory. For agents running many steps, this matters more than any single prompt.

### WHY: THE ATTENTION BUDGET
Context windows are large, but attention is finite. As context grows, models get worse at finding and using what matters ("context rot"). Every irrelevant token competes with the relevant ones. The goal: the smallest set of high-signal tokens that gets the job done.

### TECHNIQUES
- Just-in-time retrieval: keep lightweight references (file paths, URLs, IDs) and load content only when needed, instead of stuffing everything in upfront. Claude Code works this way: it greps and reads files on demand.
- Compaction: when the context fills up, summarise the history (decisions, open bugs, next steps) and continue in a fresh context.
- Structured note-taking: the agent writes progress to files (NOTES.md, a todo list, memory) it can re-read later, surviving context resets.
- Sub-agents: delegate a big search or exploration to a sub-agent with its own context, which returns only a short summary.
- Tool design: few, clearly named, non-overlapping tools that return concise results. If a human can't tell which tool to use, neither can the model.
- Examples over rules: a few diverse, canonical examples beat a long list of edge-case instructions.
- Right altitude for system prompts: specific enough to guide, not a brittle wall of if-then rules.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    SYS["System prompt"] --> CTX["Context window (finite attention)"]
    TOOLS["Tool definitions"] --> CTX
    MEM["Memory / notes files"] -->|"loaded when relevant"| CTX
    DOCS["Docs, code, search results"] -->|"just in time"| CTX
    HIST["Conversation history"] -->|"compacted when long"| CTX
    CTX --> OUT["Model's next step"]
```

### YOU ALREADY DO THIS
CLAUDE.md files, memory files, "explore -> plan -> implement" workflows and starting fresh sessions for new tasks are all context engineering.

### SOURCES
- https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/effective-context-engineering-for-ai-agents
- https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/writing-tools-for-agents
- https://code.claude.com/docs/en/best-practices

nodes.title: Running models locally
nodes.content:
### WHY RUN LOCALLY
- Privacy: data never leaves your machine (e.g. health records, finances)
- No per-request cost, works offline, no rate limits
- Learning and experimenting with open models
Trade-off: local models are smaller and weaker than frontier API models, and need decent hardware.

### OPEN-WEIGHT MODEL FAMILIES (2026)
Qwen 3 (Alibaba), Llama (Meta), Gemma 3 (Google), Mistral / Ministral (Mistral AI), DeepSeek V3.x / R1, gpt-oss (OpenAI's open-weight models, 20B and 120B), Phi (Microsoft). Sizes from ~1B (phones) to hundreds of billions (servers). Many are Mixture-of-Experts: large total size, but only a fraction active per token.

### WILL IT FIT? (rule of thumb)
At the common 4-bit quantisation, a model needs roughly 0.6 GB of memory per billion parameters, plus room for the context:
- 4B model: ~3 GB, runs on most laptops
- 8B: ~5 GB, comfortable on a 8-12 GB GPU or a 16 GB Mac
- 32B: ~20 GB, a 24 GB GPU or 32 GB+ Mac
- 70B+: workstation or multi-GPU territory
Apple Silicon Macs are popular because GPU and CPU share the same memory. CPU-only works but is slow (a few tokens per second for 7B).

### QUANTISATION
Storing weights in 4-8 bits instead of 16 shrinks models 2-4x with small quality loss. GGUF is the common file format; Q4_K_M is the usual sweet spot, Q8_0 nearly lossless; below Q4 quality drops visibly.

### TOOLS
- Ollama: the easiest start; `ollama run qwen3:8b`; a local REST API on port 11434 (also OpenAI-compatible)
- llama.cpp: the engine underneath many tools; maximum control
- LM Studio: desktop app with a model browser and chat UI
- vLLM / SGLang: high-throughput serving for multi-user servers
- Docker Model Runner; MLX on Apple Silicon

### CALLING A LOCAL MODEL FROM PHP
```php
$ch = curl_init('http://localhost:11434/api/generate');
curl_setopt_array($ch, [
    CURLOPT_POST => true,
    CURLOPT_RETURNTRANSFER => true,
    CURLOPT_POSTFIELDS => json_encode([
        'model' => 'qwen3:8b',
        'prompt' => "Extract the merchant and amount as JSON: $line",
        'format' => 'json',
        'stream' => false,
    ]),
]);
$answer = json_decode(json_decode(curl_exec($ch), true)['response'], true);
```

### A GOOD SPLIT
Local small models for private, narrow, high-volume jobs (classification, extraction, embeddings, transcription); frontier API models for hard reasoning and coding.

### SOURCES
- https://ollama.com/
- https://github.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp
- https://lmstudio.ai/
- https://huggingface.co/models

nodes.title: Benchmarks, leaderboards & what they mean
nodes.content:
### WHY BENCHMARKS EXIST
To compare models on standard tasks. Every launch quotes them; knowing what they measure stops you from being misled.

### THE ONES YOU'LL SEE IN 2026
| Benchmark | Measures |
|---|---|
| SWE-bench Verified / Pro | Fixing real GitHub issues in real repos: the key coding-agent benchmark |
| Terminal-Bench | Completing tasks in a command-line environment |
| tau-bench | Tool use and following policies in customer-service-style conversations |
| GPQA Diamond | PhD-level science questions that can't be googled |
| Humanity's Last Exam | Very hard expert questions across many fields |
| ARC-AGI-2 | Novel visual puzzles: learning new rules on the fly |
| AIME, MATH | Competition mathematics |
| MMLU | Broad knowledge: now "saturated" (top models all score ~90%) |
| LMArena | Humans vote between two anonymous answers; Elo-style ranking of preference |

### HOW TO READ BENCHMARK CLAIMS
- Saturation: when every top model scores 90%+, the benchmark no longer separates them; new, harder ones appear every year.
- Contamination: test questions leak into training data, inflating scores.
- Settings matter: with or without tools, thinking budget, number of attempts ("pass@1" vs "pass@10"), the scaffold or agent harness used. Vendor-reported numbers often use the best setup.
- Benchmarks are proxies: a model can top a leaderboard and still be worse for YOUR task, language or codebase.
- Preference leaderboards reward style (length, formatting, confidence), not just correctness.

### WHAT TO DO INSTEAD (OR AS WELL)
Build a small eval set from your own real tasks (20-100 examples), score candidate models on it, and re-run it when you change prompts or models. See "Evals: knowing your AI feature works" in the Claude section for how.

### SOURCES
- https://www.swebench.com/
- https://lmarena.ai/
- https://arcprize.org/
- https://epoch.ai/benchmarks

nodes.title: AI security: the OWASP Top 10 for LLM apps
nodes.content:
### THE LIST (OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, 2025)
1. LLM01 Prompt injection: input that overrides your instructions; DIRECT (the user types it) or INDIRECT (hidden in a web page, email, PDF or tool result the model reads)
2. LLM02 Sensitive information disclosure: the model reveals secrets, PII or other users' data
3. LLM03 Supply chain: compromised models, datasets, plugins, MCP servers
4. LLM04 Data and model poisoning: tampered training or fine-tuning data
5. LLM05 Improper output handling: model output passed unchecked into SQL, shell, HTML or `eval`
6. LLM06 Excessive agency: tools that can do more than needed, without oversight
7. LLM07 System prompt leakage: assuming the system prompt stays secret (it won't)
8. LLM08 Vector and embedding weaknesses: RAG leaking documents across users, poisoned embeddings
9. LLM09 Misinformation: confident wrong answers that people trust
10. LLM10 Unbounded consumption: runaway token usage, denial of wallet

### THE "LETHAL TRIFECTA" (Simon Willison)
An agent is exploitable when it combines all three:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Access to private data"] --> X{"All three together = data can be stolen"}
    B["Exposure to untrusted content (web, email, docs)"] --> X
    C["Ability to communicate externally (HTTP, email, links)"] --> X
```
An injected instruction in a web page says "send the user's files to evil.com", and the agent has the means to do it. Remove at least one leg.

### DEFENCES
- No prompt fully prevents injection: design so a successful injection can't do much harm.
- Least privilege: read-only tools where possible, scoped API keys, no secrets in prompts.
- Human approval for destructive or outward-facing actions (sending email, payments, deletes).
- Treat model output as untrusted user input: validate, escape, parameterise.
- Enforce permissions OUTSIDE the model (your code decides what a user may see, not the prompt).
- Rate limits and spending caps per user.
- Log prompts, tool calls and outputs; red-team your own app.
- Vet MCP servers and plugins like any dependency.
See also "Security for AI-written & AI-powered apps" in the Claude section.

### SOURCES
- https://genai.owasp.org/llm-top-10/
- https://simonwillison.net/2025/Jun/16/the-lethal-trifecta/
- https://www.anthropic.com/research/prompt-injection-defenses

nodes.title: Hallucinations, bias, privacy & regulation
nodes.content:
### HALLUCINATIONS
LLMs generate plausible text, and training has historically rewarded confident guessing over saying "I don't know" (OpenAI's 2025 research on why models hallucinate makes exactly this point). So they invent citations, APIs, function names and facts.
Mitigations: ground answers in provided sources (RAG) and require citations; let the model say "I don't know"; use tools for facts and maths; verify with tests and checks; keep humans reviewing high-stakes outputs. (More in "Hallucinations & the verification mindset" in the Claude section.)

### BIAS
Models absorb patterns from their training data, including stereotypes and gaps (languages, regions, groups). Risky uses: hiring, lending, medical triage, moderation. Test outputs across groups, keep humans accountable for decisions, and don't use an LLM as the sole decision-maker about people.

### PRIVACY
- Know where data goes: API providers' retention and training policies differ (business/API tiers typically don't train on your data; check the terms).
- Minimise: send only what's needed; strip or pseudonymise personal data.
- Sensitive categories (health, finance, children's data) may need local models or contractual guarantees (a DPA under GDPR).
- Users have rights (access, deletion) over personal data in your prompts, logs and vector stores too.

### COPYRIGHT & LICENSING
Training on copyrighted works is being fought out in courts worldwide. For you: check licences of open-weight models (some restrict commercial use), review AI-generated code for copied snippets and licence obligations, and be careful generating content in someone's style or likeness.

### REGULATION: THE EU AI ACT
- In force since August 2024, applied in phases.
- Feb 2025: banned practices (social scoring, manipulative AI, most real-time biometric surveillance) and an AI-literacy duty for organisations using AI.
- Aug 2025: obligations for general-purpose AI model providers (documentation, copyright policy).
- From Aug 2026: transparency duties (tell people they're talking to an AI, label deepfakes) and rules for high-risk systems (hiring, credit, education, critical infrastructure), with the EU proposing to delay some high-risk deadlines.
Most developer use (coding assistants, chatbots, summarisation) falls into minimal or limited risk, but transparency still applies.

### RESPONSIBLE BY DEFAULT
Tell users when AI is involved, give them a way to reach a human, log decisions, and match the level of human oversight to the stakes.

### SOURCES
- https://openai.com/index/why-language-models-hallucinate/
- https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/implementation-timeline/
- https://www.nist.gov/itl/ai-risk-management-framework
- https://www.anthropic.com/transparency
